s01.slug: MONDAY · 6:50 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: The light comes in gray over the sill and finds the floorboards first, then the heap of their clothes, then the white wall above the mattress, going from gray to white as it climbs. Below the bluff the surf is still big from the weekend, breaking and pulling back under everything.

body.text: He wakes in her bed with the day already in the room. Not Ellery, not the Saab at the Rincon, not six o’clock in December with the dark still on and two boards to load: her bed, the morning on the wall, her knee over his.
body.else: He came back down Del Playa at six with the dark just lifting, and she let him in at the door in his flannel and went back to sleep on him before he had his shoes off. Now the morning is on the wall, and her knee is over his.

body: Downstairs Tomás’s coffee grinder starts up through the floor, a dentist in the next town, and stops, and starts again. The room is cold everywhere the sheet isn’t.
She’s awake. She’s lying on her side with her cheek on her arm, watching him, and from the look of her she’s been at it for some time.

body.text: “Still now?” she says.
“Still here?” she says.

body: “Yes,” he says, and the word is already out in the room with the light by the time he hears it.

She has a Sharpie from somewhere. She always has a Sharpie from somewhere. She pulls the cap off with her teeth, pushes the sheet down off his ribs with the back of her hand, and says around the cap, “Hold still. I’m finishing.”

Her fingers have been drawing on him in her sleep. Now she means it. The felt tip is cold and wet and tickles like hell, and he isn’t allowed to laugh, because she’s working, the cap clamped in her teeth and her hair down over one eye. It’s a horse. It has a mane this time, and a tail with some wind in it, and four legs that bend the way legs go, and last, with the very tip, an eye. She sits back to look at it.
Under the horse, smaller and worse, she adds a lily: three petals and a band across their middle, the left one leaning like it’s had a couple.
“That’s a fleur-de-lis,” he says.
“It’s a lily.” Through the cap. “I did the reading.” She blows on it to dry it, one long cool breath from his ribs to his hip, and he looks very hard at the ceiling.
“You’re blushing on your ribs,” she says, interested. “I didn’t know you could do that there.”

The RAZR is in his jeans on the floor. He fishes it out one-handed. Theo’s from 11:58 last night is still waiting on the little outside screen — *Home? Asking for Hollis.* — and he answers it now, with her chin on his shoulder, reading along.

body.text: home. eventually.

body: “*Eventually*,” Skye reads. “Such commitment.” She takes the cap out of her mouth. “Corinne at nine. An hour on the phone about my face. Then I’m putting myself on tape.”
“For what?”
“A pilot.”
“What pilot?”
“I don’t say it till I have it. It’s bad luck. Actors are worse than Catholics.”
“My grandmother would light a candle on it.”
“Your grandmother already has a candle going on me.” She sounds very pleased about it. “What have you got?”
“Hale at one.” He shuts the phone. “Come get me after?”
“I’m taking you somewhere with a parking meter.”
“What’s there?”
“A meter, Jack. Bring quarters.”
Tomás’s voice comes up the stairwell. “Skye. Coffee.” The clink of a mug on the rail. “Point’s closing out. Somebody put white ones at the cross again.” His feet go back down.

“Thanks, Tomás,” she calls. Her eyes have gone to the floor by the mattress, where Sunday left his clothes: the jeans with the bulletin still folded in the back pocket, the T-shirt, the Marisol sweatshirt inside out.
“You have to wear those,” she says. “The Mass clothes. It’s tradition.”
“Whose tradition?”

“The street’s. Del Playa at seven in the morning, in your church clothes, past every boy on the block hosing last night off his porch. I’ll narrate.” She comes up on one elbow with the sheet held to her chest and drops into the hush of a man lying in the grass with binoculars. “*Dawn, on the Central Coast. The young male stirs. He does not yet know what awaits him.*”
She breaks off. “Is there a saint for this? There’s a saint for everything.”
“Augustine,” Jack says. “The famous one. *Lord, make me chaste —*”
“*— but not yet.*” She points the Sharpie at him. “That one I know. It was on a mug in a makeup trailer. Somebody’s ex-wife gave it to him. I like Augustine. He was honest about his calendar.”
“He got there,” Jack says. “Eventually.”
“Don’t.” She caps the pen. “I like him how he is.”
She lies back down with her head on his shoulder and her hair across his mouth.
“Anyway,” she says, “shame’s Wednesday. Today’s just the walk.”
He puts his hand in her hair and leaves it. Downstairs the grinder stops.
She sits up. “So. The walk. Who’s doing the voice?”

response: She follows him down as far as the porch in his sweatshirt and very little else, and does the rest from the top step in the binocular hush. “*The male, having failed to migrate, attempts the journey home in his Sunday plumage. Note the bulletin. Note the gait. He has been to church, and then he has very much not been to church.*”

Two houses down a boy hosing sand off his steps lets the hose go slack. “*A rival male,*” she breathes. “*He senses weakness.*” She keeps it up past the third house and the fourth, over the surf and the grinder, and when Jack gets to the corner he bows to Ocean Road without turning around, and hears her lose it behind him.

He does it himself, from her doorway, getting into the jeans, in the flattest Youngstown he owns. “*The young Catholic emerges, blinking. He is a long way from his parish. Mrs. Fitch will hear of this by noon. He will say he was at a Bible study. He will not be believed.*”

“*By nine*,” Skye corrects him, from under the sheet. “*Mrs. Fitch hears of it by nine.*” He pulls the sweatshirt over his head, and the horse on his ribs is the last thing she sees of him before the sweatshirt comes down over it. On the stairs a sock hits him between the shoulder blades. It’s his.

She’s drawing breath for the next line when he leans down and kisses her in the middle of a word, and the binoculars go, and the hush, and her hand goes into his hair and keeps him there until the documentary is a lost cause. Her thumb finds the scar in his eyebrow on the way.
“Go,” she says into his mouth. “Go before I cast you.”
“As what?”
“The male.”
He goes. Every stair on the way down tells Tomás about it, and Tomás, at the grinder, lifts his mug to him without a word.

body: The sun gets into 412 at a quarter past eight, through the one window, and lays itself across Theo’s half of the room first, because Theo’s half is where the good furniture is. Through the wall Doug’s alarm begins the argument it has with Doug every morning, a car horn on a nine-minute snooze, and loses.

Theo is at his desk, dressed, the blue blazer on and the Sigma Rho pin set into the lapel at the exact angle three brothers told him to. On the nightstand Hollis keeps his retirement in the teacup. “Hollis was concerned,” Theo says, to the MacBook, as Jack comes in. “I told him you’d been detained by the Holy See.”
Jack is in yesterday’s Mass jeans and the Marisol sweatshirt, under the Carhartt. It is not a look that has ever fooled anyone, least of all an egg.
“He’s an egg.”

“He is a *retired* egg, Costigan, and he keeps vigil. It’s all he has left.” Theo looks up then, with a question in his face, and Jack waits for it. Theo folds it small and puts it away somewhere inside the blazer. “Seven hours after I asked,” he says instead. “*Home. Eventually.* One of them is a hedge.”
“It was accurate.”

“It was a confession. Sit. Your Englishman wrote.” He turns the MacBook around on the desk. Jack has never owned a laptop, so his Marisol e-mail lives on Theo’s, in a second window, and behind it is a window with the President’s budget in it, $3.8 trillion and a three-year freeze, which Theo shuts as if it had asked him for money. “Saturday, to all twelve of you. I took the liberty. You didn’t check.”

He reads it aloud before Jack can, in Hale’s vowels. He does them well: the Oxford pressed flat like a flower between the clauses, and a pause after *ambitions* where Hale would take a sip of something.

body.title: PHIL 109H — Monday
body.text: For Monday, in place of what the syllabus says: Joyce, “The Dead.” It is a long story with ambitions. Read it twice. No sides; for once you will all simply read. —A.H.

body: “*No sides*,” Theo says, in his own voice, and sets the phrase down between them like a ceasefire. “Joyce. I have a copy, from a previous owner who found Gabriel Conroy SO CONDESCENDING, in green ink, and was correct. Don’t let her opinions near yours.” He gets the Penguin off the shelf over his bed and puts it in Jack’s hand. “Forty-odd pages, twice. It is the greatest short story in English and it has a goose in it, so pace yourself. You have five hours and, I’m told, a soul.”
The word *Wednesday* is in neither of them. They both go around it.
At the door, bag on his shoulder, blazer squared, Theo turns. “Six days, Costigan.”
Jack doesn’t ask till what. Everyone in Delgado can count to Sunday.

He reads at his desk with the door propped open, the way he read at Glenwood, with other people’s noise leaking in at the edges, and by the time Doug’s alarm has lost for the fourth time he has met a girl named Lily, who is already run off her feet, and a man named Gabriel, who is already worried about his speech.

Hollis 302 gets the sun after lunch. It comes in low and white off the water through the three tall windows and falls in bars across the oak, over a dozen paperbacks open to the same forty pages, and puts a glare on every one of them.

Hale comes in with no coat, no dog and no remark. He has a *Dubliners* with a green spine, cracked so many times at the last story that it falls open there by itself, and he sits where he sat a week ago, halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end. Evan is at the door with the roster on its clipboard, and the pen goes click down the names.
“Good afternoon,” Hale says, as he says it on any Monday of the year, and it’s the most frightening thing Jack has heard out of him.

“Joyce,” he says, “wrote this in Trieste, at twenty-five, broke, having been extremely rude to everybody he knew in Dublin. It’s the last story in the book and the only kind one. Some people think it’s an apology. If it is, it’s the best sort: it never says sorry.” He turns a page he doesn’t need to turn. “We shan’t take sides. We shall simply read. I appreciate it will be a novelty.”

Jack has the door end, under the clock. Lena has the window end, where she has had it every seminar since January. Her book is squared to the edge of the table with the pencil laid across it, and that is as far down the table as he looks.

He read it twice, because the email said twice: once at his desk with Doug’s alarm losing through the wall, and the last six pages again on the Hollis stairs ten minutes ago, standing up, with people going around him. Under his shirt there’s a horse on his ribs in Sharpie that a Delgado shower didn’t touch, and he can feel exactly where it is. There are six real ones in his jeans, from the change machine in the Commons, for a parking meter.

It’s all there in the forty pages: a party at a warm house in the dead of the year, two old aunts and a piano and too much food; a clever woman who quarrels with the favorite nephew in the middle of a dance over a name she calls him, and has her hat and cloak on and is gone before supper; the speech he gets up and gives after the goose, polished all night; a wife who hears a song on the stairs at the end of the evening and is gone, years back, to a boy in the rain, while her husband finds out in a hotel room, when there is nothing left to do with it but lie there and listen to the snow. Caleb and Yusuf were there Wednesday. Most of the rest have heard some version. Nobody at the oak looks at either end of it.
Twelve people turn the page at once. At the door Evan’s pen has stopped clicking.
“Was Miss Ivors right about Gabriel?” Hale asks the room.

A sophomore from the window side says Miss Ivors was rude. True. Somebody else says Gabriel writes for the wrong paper and knows it; Joyce made sure of it. Caleb, on Jack’s side of the table, has been having the time of his life since the email; he has his Joyce up in front of his face like a hymnal and a smile aimed straight down into it, and he says into the pages, at the volume he believes is a whisper, “*West Briton.*”

Hale lets it go. He finds the place instead and reads it to them, Gabriel and Miss Ivors going down the room together in the dance, and the name coming out of her at the end of it: “*West Briton!*” He does it in a voice like a hatpin, and puts the book down.
“But she’s right,” says one of the girls from the window side. “He’s a snob. He’s embarrassed by all of them.”
“She’s right and she’s horrible,” says the other.

“The two are very often found together,” says Hale. “Like gin and quinine.” He turns his head neither way. “Miss Ivors is the only person in that house who says precisely what she thinks, and Joyce sends her home without her supper for it. Draw no conclusions. What did Gabriel get wrong about the evening — the speech, or the wife?”

“The speech. Lo,” Caleb says, before anybody else can. “He toasts his aunts like they’re already dead. Kind old ladies, the good old days, everybody who isn’t here anymore. It’s a eulogy with a fork in it.”
“Hargrove has made a point,” says Hale, “in the vernacular, which is the only place points are ever made. Anyone else?”

Yusuf takes it. On Wednesday night he was in Hale’s kitchen with the lid still on his coffee, and this hour he has answered every question about the snow and not one about the party, and he answers this one about the snow too. “Neither. The weather. It’s at the door when Gabriel comes in, it’s on the window while he waits to talk, it’s on the hotel glass at the end. Same load on every roof in Ireland.” He shrugs. “It’s the only thing in the story that treats them all the same.”
“Mr. Noorzai has found the one egalitarian in Dublin,” says Hale, “and it’s precipitation.”
At the window end Lena takes the pencil off her book.

“The wife,” she says. “Gretta has carried a boy who died for her through a whole marriage, two children and a house in Monkstown, and nobody knew; one song on the stairs at the end of the night and she is gone to him, years back, in the rain, and the husband who has watched her all evening, who is sure he is what she’s thinking about, sees nothing at all. And then Joyce gives the last page to him, as though it were his to have.”
Hale looks at her long enough to say “Yes,” and turns his head the other way.
Jack turns a page. It’s a reading of Joyce, and not a bad one. He has Miss Ivors in the hall with her cloak half buttoned, pencil-marked, and he goes back to her.
“Why,” Hale asks, “does she leave before the goose?”

A sophomore at the window side, who wasn’t at anybody’s house on Wednesday, laughs at *goose*, because it is a funny word. It’s a nice laugh. It goes out over the oak by itself, and it doesn’t find anybody, and she stops and looks hard at her book.

The question stays on the table with the sun on it. It doesn’t go to the window end. It comes down the oak chair by chair, Caleb, Yusuf, the girl who laughed, each of them finding something to read, until it’s sitting in front of Jack, and the room is looking at the clock over his head.

choices.text: “Miss Ivors was right about Gabriel. She was wrong to say it in his aunts’ house.”
response: “She’s right about all of it,” Jack says. “He *is* looking east. He writes for the paper she says he writes for, he’d sooner go cycling in France than see Galway, and he knows it, that’s why it stings. She’s right.” He turns the page back to her. “And she says it in the middle of a dance, at his aunts’ party, where he can’t answer her without spoiling the night for two old women who’ve been cooking since Christmas. So she goes before the goose. She can’t sit down and eat their food after that. She knows what she did.”

The table takes it without a word. At the window end Lena’s pencil stops on the page. Caleb lowers his Joyce to look at Jack over the top of it, and slowly raises it again. Jack is watching Hale, and Hale nods, slowly, to the book.

He reads the end himself: the snow on the plain and the hills and the dark water of the Shannon, on the graveyard on the hill where the boy is buried, and then the last sentence, unhurried, each word set down where it goes. “*His soul swooned slowly as he heard the snow falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling, like the descent of their last end, upon all the living and the dead.*”
He shuts the book on his finger. “Miss Broussard, a moment. Mr. Costigan — the corridor. I’ll want you after.”

choices.text: “Gabriel’s real sin is the speech. He workshopped it.”
response: “Gabriel’s real sin is the speech,” Jack says. “He workshopped it. He’s been running it since the coats came off. He’s got the Browning in, then he takes the Browning out because it’ll go over their heads, then he puts in a line about hospitality for the aunts. Miss Ivors leaves before the goose so she doesn’t have to sit through the draft.”
The table laughs, harder than it’s funny: an hour’s worth, all at once. Caleb smacks the oak. Even Yusuf laughs, into his coffee.
Hale doesn’t laugh. “He did,” he says. “In front of the mirror, I expect. Go on, someone.”

Jack has more of it, the toast to the three Graces, the part where he swears off the past and then can’t stop talking about it, and he can feel it ready in his mouth, the next one and the one after, as it always is. Hale is looking at him over the top of the room with nothing in his face at all, and Jack keeps the rest.

No one goes on. The laugh runs down by itself, and in what’s left of it Hale reads the end of the story aloud to them, the snow coming down on the living and the dead, and closes the book and lays it flat on the oak with the green spine toward the windows. “Miss Broussard, a moment. Mr. Costigan — the corridor. I’ll want you after.”

choices.text: *Say nothing about Miss Ivors. Talk about the snow.*
response: He leaves Miss Ivors where she is, and gives them the snow. It’s on Gabriel’s galoshes when he comes in, the ones Gretta makes fun of. It’s on the window he stands at while the others dance. It’s outside the Gresham at the end, *general all over Ireland*, Jack says, the kind of thing a newspaper would say, and Joyce takes the newspaper’s sentence and makes it mean the dead and the living under the same weather: the aunts, and the boy in Galway, and Gabriel at the glass, none of them kept out of it and none of them spared.

Yusuf looks up at him from the corner, for the first time all hour. Caleb, who was waiting for something else, lowers his Joyce and looks disappointed in him, and raises it again. Hale’s eyes stay on Jack a second longer than the answer needs.

Then Hale reads them the end, slowly, to the last of it — “*upon all the living and the dead*” — and leaves the book open on the oak, face up in the sun. “Miss Broussard, a moment. Mr. Costigan — the corridor. I’ll want you after.”

choices.text: “Gabriel’s whole night is him finding out he was never the subject.”
response: “Gabriel’s whole night is him finding out he was never the subject,” Jack says. “Miss Ivors goes because he isn’t worth staying for. The speech is about him. The aunts are about him. He gets up to the hotel thinking the night was building up to him, and it was about a boy in the rain all along.”

The room goes quiet. It’s the kind of quiet where people find out they’ve been holding their pens too hard. Caleb puts his book down. One of the window-side girls looks at the door end and then, fast, at the other end, and then at her lap. At the window end Lena looks at the window.

Hale pushes his reading glasses up into his hair, where he will lose them by four o’clock, and gives them the end from memory, without the book: the snow on the plain and the hills and the Shannon, on the graveyard where the boy is buried, falling faintly, and faintly falling, *upon all the living and the dead*. He gets every word. Then he looks down the table at the clock, and not at either end of it. “Miss Broussard, a moment. Mr. Costigan — the corridor. I’ll want you after.”

s03a.slug: MONDAY · 2:31 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE THIRD-FLOOR CORRIDOR
body: The third-floor corridor is old red tile and a drinking fountain that hums, and at the end of it is 314, HALE on the pebbled glass in gold leaf that has been coming off the H for years. Through the glass there are two shapes and two voices, his low and level, hers lower, and nothing Jack could repeat if somebody asked him. He doesn’t try. He leans on the wall by the fountain with his bag at his feet and Theo’s Penguin in his back pocket, the previous owner’s green capitals still shouting in its margins, and he reads the corkboard: a lost bike, an Oxford summer program, a colloquium on Kierkegaard with Evan’s name on it in smaller type than the title. Behind him 302 empties onto the tile. The window-side girls go by with their heads together and stop talking as they pass him, and start again at the stairs. Yusuf comes last with his empty cup and gives Jack a nod aimed at about the level of his shoes, and keeps going.

It takes six minutes by the clock over the stairwell. The door opens and Lena comes out with her bag already on her shoulder before it’s shut behind her, and her face set, and she walks past him close enough that her coat stirs the flyers, and doesn’t look at him.
It’s over, and he’s glad it’s over. He’s irritated, too, with himself, for standing right where she had to pass him to get to the stairs, with a corridor the length of the building to stand in.
“Mr. Costigan.”

Hale’s office has the Pacific in the window and the green carpet with the wine stain shaped like Italy. The radiator under the sill is cold. There’s a leash on the hook behind the door, and under the desk Berkeley’s blanket is still holding the long dent of a dog. On the desk: a coffee ring on a blue book, the Housman, the green *Dubliners* face down, and under the *Dubliners* a small black book, very old, the spine gone soft as cloth.

Hale sits. He doesn’t offer the other chair. Jack stands with his bag on his shoulder in front of the desk; he has stood in front of desks before, nuns’ desks mostly, and knows to keep his hands out of his pockets.

body.text: “Right about Gabriel, wrong in his aunts’ house,” Hale says. “You knew exactly whose house you were in when you said it.”
“He workshopped it,” Hale says. “Very good. You got a laugh. You’re always going to get the laugh, Mr. Costigan. It’s the least interesting thing about you.”
“The snow,” Hale says. “Very wise. Very Irish. You’ve learned to talk about the weather.”
“Never the subject,” Hale says. “That was well put and very badly timed.”

body: He folds his hands on the blue book. Monday has nothing of the north in his voice; it’s all Oxford, dry and exact, every consonant paid for.

“I taught that story at you today,” he says. “You noticed. Everybody noticed; Mr. Hargrove noticed out loud. That is what a seminar is, Mr. Costigan. Twelve people agreeing to notice the same thing at the same time and keep their hands to themselves.”
“You could have just said it,” Jack says. “In there.”

“To the pair of you? With an audience?” Hale’s eyebrows go up a fraction. “You’d have been delighted. You’re both at your very best with an audience, which is most of what’s wrong with you. No. In there you read Joyce. In here you get me.”
“I have had a great many arguments at that table, Mr. Costigan. Until Wednesday not one of them had sent the dog under the kitchen table.”
Somewhere below the window a mower starts, and stops.
“You went for the places that hurt. You’re good at it.” A fact, as he’d write it in a margin, and not a compliment. “I’d rather you weren’t.”

body.text: “*A clipboard*,” he says, as if reading it off the ceiling. “That was yours.”
“*A man who agrees with everything she says*,” he says, as if reading it off the ceiling. “That was yours.”
Hale doesn’t name it. He has no need to.
“I don’t care which of you was telling the truth about a telephone. I care that you did it to win.”
body.else: “I don’t care which of you was right about Graham Greene. I care that you did it to win.”

body: Jack can think of four answers to that, standing there, and every one of them would win.
“What I had to say to Miss Broussard I’ve said, and you won’t have it from me.” He lifts one hand off the blue book and sets it down again. “Nor from her, I should think.”
He turns his chair a few degrees toward the water.
“Miss Ivors left before the goose. Nobody at that party remembers what she was right about. Everyone remembers she left.”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. Monday he gave us Joyce, “The Dead,” and taught it as if Wednesday never happened, and everybody at the table knew what it was for. He kept Lena after with the door shut. Then me: until Wednesday no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table. He said I went for the places that hurt, that I’m good at it, and that he’d rather I weren’t. Miss Ivors left before the goose. Nobody remembers what she was right about.

choices.key: In his office Hale said no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table before Wednesday. You told him Lena called you a liar first.
response: Hale turns back from the window.
“And you’d like that on the record,” he says. “It isn’t a record. It’s a dinner.”

He picks the *Dubliners* up off the desk, gets up, and opens the door for Jack himself, and stands holding it with the book in his other hand. Jack goes out past him into the corridor with exactly what he came in with.

choices.key: In his office Hale said no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table before Wednesday. You said, ‘Yes, sir.’
response: “Don’t *sir* me. I’m not a bishop and you’re not sorry.”

But he tips his head at the door, and there’s no edge on it at all, and from Hale that is as near as a dismissal comes to kind. Jack goes. Behind him, before the door is shut, he hears the *Dubliners* fall open on the desk at the place it always falls open.

choices.text: “Then don’t seat us at the same table.”
choices.key: In his office Hale said no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table before Wednesday. You told him not to seat you at the same table. He said you’re the only two worth sitting at it.
response: Hale looks at him across the desk for some time.
“I seat you at the same table,” he says, “because you’re the only two who make it worth sitting at.”
He slides the blue book out from under the coffee ring, uncaps a pen, and starts on somebody’s essay. Jack is in the corridor before he’s finished the first margin.

choices.text: “It won’t happen in your house again.”
choices.key: In his office Hale said no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table before Wednesday. You told him it won’t happen in his house again. He said that isn’t what he asked.
response: “That isn’t what I asked.”
Jack waits to be told what was. Hale takes his time. He looks down past his own knees at the blanket under the desk, at the long shallow dent in it, and keeps whatever he did ask where it is.

s03b.slug: MONDAY · 2:44 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE FRONT STAIRS
body: Caleb is on the second-floor landing with his back against the window and his bag on both shoulders, waiting for him on purpose.
“That was *Joyce*, Costigan.” He comes off the window and falls in a step above Jack, going down, lit up. “He assigned *Joyce* at you.”
“He assigned it at twelve people.”
“And the twelve,” says Caleb, “were sore afraid.” He stops on the turn of the stairs. “Who was I? Be honest. Was I the drunk one?”
“You were Freddy Malins.”
“I had *one glass*.” He peels off at the first floor toward the vending machines, still delighted, saying *West Briton* to himself in an accent from no country on earth.

Julian Park-Ellis is at the foot of the stairs in one of his father’s cardigans, with Lena’s bag over his shoulder, and Lena beside him doing up the buttons of her coat. The building has been telling a version of Wednesday since Thursday morning, and if he’s heard one, from her or from the halls, none of it is in his face. He gets the heavy front door for her, the guitar calluses white on the brass bar. She goes through it without looking back.

Jack is three steps behind, and Julian sees him coming and keeps the door where it is. He holds it for Jack too, and nods, a small, decent nod, as if they were two people who happen to be leaving the same building.
Jack nods back.

Outside, in the flat bright afternoon, Evan Marsh is on the bench by the bike racks with a coffee going cold beside him and an American Spirit he hasn’t lit, watching the two of them go off down the walk toward Del Playa. When Jack comes past the bench Evan’s eyes leave them and settle on him: a long look, tired and Minnesotan, over the wire glasses. Evan goes back to watching the walk.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight. In sixty-one pictures from Lucille’s baptism, at the Broussards’ table between Mémère and Josie. Tess’s caption calls him *le petit violon*. Flew home to Oakland on the fourth. Tuesday morning, on the feed: a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late; Lena tagged. Songs for Haiti, Friday at Bastille, every dollar to CRS. Theo asked him how many are about her. ‘One.’ At Sully’s Lena introduced him to Skye. ‘The flyers.’ Theo says the new one is about a river. Monday he was at the foot of the Hollis stairs with her bag on his shoulder. He held the door for her, and then for me.

s03c.slug: MONDAY · 2:50 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE BACK STEPS
body: The back steps have had the sun on them since noon, and so have the loading dock and the dumpster with the dolphin painted on it. Somebody has given the dolphin a handlebar mustache since Friday. Jack sits on the second step with his bag between his feet. The concrete is warm through his jeans. A delivery truck is backing up to the Commons kitchen with its beeper going, and the quarters shift in his pocket when he leans back on his elbows.
*Everyone remembers she left.* He was on the deck when she did. He doesn’t need it twice.
He has the pack out of the inside pocket of the Carhartt, and doesn’t remember going in after it. The lighter is in with it. In the other pocket, against his hip, is the tin.

choices.key: After Hale’s, on the back steps, you smoked one.
response: He lights it with his shoulder to the warm stucco and smokes it the way he smokes now, fast and hard, half of it in five pulls, tasting none of it. The Saab’s horn goes from around the far side of the loading dock in the middle of a drag, two short taps, and he coughs smoke out over the dolphin and laughs at himself, and puts it out on the step, and puts the end in his pocket on his way down.

He puts the pack back down into the lining and sits there on the warm concrete with both hands jammed in the Carhartt till they quit wanting anything. It takes longer than he’d like. Around the far side of the loading dock the Saab’s horn goes twice, the second one going up at the end, like a question, and he picks up his bag.
He puts the pack away and takes out the tin. RELIQUARY, on the lid, in marker. He opens it on his knee in the sun and counts them with one fingertip.
Eleven. He knew it was eleven.
He shuts it. The click of the lid is louder than the Saab’s horn, coming from around the far side of the loading dock right on top of it, and the tin is back in his pocket before he’s on his feet.

He puts the pack away and takes out the tin and counts them on his knee in the sun. Eleven, same as always. He shuts it on the sound of the Saab’s horn from around the far side of the loading dock, and it’s back in his pocket before he stands up.

s04.slug: MONDAY · 4:00 PM · STATE STREET, SANTA BARBARA — TIDEWATER BOOKS
body: The afternoon is gold over the water when the Saab comes down off the 101 at the beach, and by then he has told her “The Dead.” She made him, on the on-ramp at Marisol, because she has never read it and wouldn’t let him summarize, so he told it properly, start to finish, from the aunts’ door to the Gresham Hotel. She drove with both hands on the wheel and interrupted twice, once to ask what galoshes were and once to say, about Gabriel, “Oh, I *hate* him,” with real pleasure.

body.text: At the light on Cabrillo she leans across and puts her nose to the collar of the Carhartt. “You had one.” “One.” She sits back and asks him what a gasworks is.

body: Coming up State he tells her why it has to be a store. Trumbull takes books only from a seller, shipped in the seller’s box, nothing handed over by family; in the fall *Brideshead* went to Danny by way of Driftwood, and the C.O. who read it first reported that it was about a house. And he tells her that before Christmas Danny walked into the prison library and asked for Flannery O’Connor, because Jack wouldn’t shut up about her across a visiting-room table. They had one story of hers, in an anthology with the cover torn off: the grandmother. Danny wrote Ma afterward that she raised peacocks and she was mean and he liked her.
“Then he’s getting the rest of her,” Skye says, and changes lanes without signaling, her version of applause.

February on State Street is seventy degrees and a little embarrassed about it: the sun along the arcades, the red tile warm to look at, a man in shorts walking a bulldog in a sweater. She parks below Carrillo in front of a meter with a dent in its head and holds out her hand, palm up. Jack puts four quarters in it. She feeds them in one at a time, watches the little red flag drop out of sight, and says, “See? I keep my promises.”
On the sidewalk she takes his arm. “Was it about the dog?”
Somebody’s version of Wednesday has made it out to Del Playa, and from the question, the version had a dog in it.
“Mostly the dog,” Jack says.
She looks at him over the top of her sunglasses for about as long as it takes a car to pass. Then she pushes them back up. “Good dog,” she says, and holds the door.

Tidewater Books is a shoebox stood on its end and pushed back from the street: narrow, deep, dim after the sidewalk, shelves to the pressed-tin ceiling and a library ladder on a brass rail to reach the top of them. A gray cat is asleep on the new hardcovers in a square of window. Behind the register, on a little stereo between a spike of receipts and a jar of pens, two acoustic guitars and a boy’s voice, sweet and very young, are coming from some year before either of them was born. The man at the register has a gray ponytail and a paperback, and he nods at them over it.
“He’s not mine,” he says, when Skye crouches to the cat. “He comes in for the window.”

She won’t let Jack help. She goes down the fiction wall on her knees with her head tipped sideways to read the spines, past the M’s and the N’s, and comes up out of the O’s with it: *The Complete Stories*, fat as a phone book, the spine never cracked. She holds it up over her head at him from the floor.
“He’s read the grandmother,” she says. “Now he gets the rest of the family.”

The man with the ponytail takes the shipping without a blink. They send to Lompoc every week, he says; once, to Folsom. He slides a form across, and Jack fills it in in his ordinary hand, the name and the number and the institution and the town, and takes a ten-pack of envelopes off the rack by the register while he’s at it, the glossy kind, because they’re there.
“Gift?” the man says.
“It’s for his brother,” Skye says. “He’s in Ohio.”
*Ohio*.

No wrapping, the man tells her, no card, nothing taped inside; they open everything. She can write on the packing slip if she wants. She wants. She takes a pen out of the jar and turns her shoulder to Jack and writes in her block letters, fast, and he gets the top line before she folds it — FOR DANNY, 23. — and then the rest goes under the fold and inside the front cover, and she settles the book in its box with both hands, like she’s tucking it in.
“What’d you write?”
“Things,” she says. “Professional things.”

While the man tapes it, she drifts back to fiction and comes out with a Penguin *Dubliners* off the shelf, and stands in the aisle reading the last pages with one finger going down the margin and her lips moving. The boy on the stereo has gone on to something else. Jack leans on the end of the shelf and doesn’t interrupt her. It costs him.
She closes it on her finger. “Okay. Gretta.”
“Gabriel.”

“No. *Gretta*.” She ticks them off on the *Dubliners*. “The aunts are doing hostess. Freddy’s doing drunk. Miss Ivors is doing Ireland. And Gabriel is doing everything — the galoshes, the speech, the quote he’s worried is too smart for the room. He’s running lines in his head all through the party. I’ve worked with that guy. I’ve *been* that guy, at a lot of parties.” She opens the book again. “And she’s on the stairs, listening to a song and thinking about a dead boy. She’s the only person in the house who’s actually where she is. He looks up and sees her and wants to paint her. He’s got a title for it. *Distant Music*.” She shuts it. “And she has to do it standing still on a stair. Do you know how hard that is? One song, start to finish, and nothing moves but your neck.”

body.text: “And then it snows,” Jack says. “On everybody. On the living and the dead, on the boy’s grave out in the west, on Gabriel at the window. It’s the first time all night he isn’t the middle of anything. He just gets to be one of the people it’s falling on. It comes from outside, it covers everybody, and he didn’t earn a flake of it.” He shrugs inside the Carhartt. “It doesn’t care who gave the speech.”
body.else: “And then it snows,” Jack says. “On everybody.” He gave Hale the rest of it at one o’clock. He shrugs inside the Carhartt. “It doesn’t care who gave the speech.”

body: She reads it to him off the page, quietly, so the man at the register can’t hear her doing it — *falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling* — and looks up.

“*I think he died for me*,” she says. “She says that to her husband in a hotel room. You can’t act that line. It’s a terrible reading. It’s just true.” She taps the last page. “He got *cast*, Jack. He spent all night auditioning for the lead, and at the end somebody finally tells him he’s the husband in a story about a boy who stood in the rain. It’s a smaller part. And it’s the first time all night he’s right for it.” She smiles at him over the book. “You can call that grace if you want. In my business it’s called getting the note.”

response: She points the *Dubliners* at him, delighted.
“Yes,” she says. “And it doesn’t take meetings.” She points the *Dubliners* at him. “But that’s mine. You’re doing my material at me. Point to me.”
He gives her the point. She puts Joyce back on the shelf spine-in, so the next person has to want it.

choices.text: “You’re right. He’s the only one acting.”
response: She holds the book against her chest and studies him a while, long enough for the boy on the stereo to finish a song.
“Don’t concede to me in a bookstore,” she says. “I’ll get used to it.”

She carries the *Dubliners* up to the register and buys it too, and has the man put it in a bag, not the box. “That one’s mine,” she tells him. “I’m going to read it with a pencil and find out I was right.”
She opens her mouth to win and, for a second, has nothing in it.

Then she does. “Then I’ve been in the wrong business,” she says, and backs him two steps into the Penguin Classics by the front of the Carhartt and kisses him, short and thorough, the *Dubliners* still open in her other hand against his back. Somewhere behind him a row of spines gives a little, and stays given.

s04a.slug: MONDAY · 4:35 PM · STATE STREET AT CARRILLO — THE RED LIGHT
body: She puts the top down outside Tidewater — the latch over the mirror, the button, the canvas folding itself back into the trunk in sections — and by Carrillo the sun is low enough to come in sideways between the buildings and lie across their laps. She’s in her gray fleece zipped to the chin and her sunglasses, her hair knotted up off her neck with a pen from the store’s jar she didn’t give back. The paper bag with his envelopes rides in the back seat. The box stayed on the counter for the UPS man, and the receipt is in Jack’s jeans with his brother’s number on it in his own hand.
The light at Carrillo goes red and she stops first in line, under a palm with a shopping cart parked at its foot.
“Danny’s twenty-three tomorrow,” Jack says.
“What do you get for twenty-three in there?”

“A phone call. Push-ups. Ma puts money on his account and he buys honey buns off the commissary sheet.” He puts his head back on the seat. “Out here you don’t get anything either. Twenty-five you get the car insurance. Twenty-three’s a layover.”

Skye watches the light. “I had my sixteenth on a soundstage in Burbank,” she says. “They wheeled out a sheet cake at lunch with my character’s name on it. Not mine. Hers. They spelled it right.” She lifts one shoulder. “I ate the corner with the most frosting. It’s a sickness.”
“Danny got his name on a cake every year till he left,” Jack says. “Ma’s handwriting. She always ran out of room before the *y* and had to go up the side.”
“So he’s been Dann his whole life.”
“With a *y* up the side.”
She takes that in like it’s a fact she’s going to need later, and nods.

The radio has been an LA station since they got in the car, fading on the curves and coming back, and it comes back now out of an ad for a mattress store and, unasked, plays it: the slow synth, the heartbeat drum, the falsetto easing in like it has all night. Skye reaches over and turns it up as far as it goes, and turns in her seat to look at him.
“It’s a *sign*,” she says.
“*An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign*,” Jack says.
“Then we’re the target audience.”

She takes the first verse. She has every word of it, and she gives it to him, not to the street and not to the car beside them: to him, eyes on his, conducting with a lime out of the cup holder. Her sunglasses go up into her hair on a high note and end up crooked and she leaves them that way. Jack has the hook from the far side of a cinderblock wall — Doug Pruitt plays this song at one in the morning more often than a man should, and Jack has lain in 412 and learned it against his will — and when it comes around he’s there for it, drumming the dash with both hands, and they hit it together at the top of their lungs, straight at each other, their eyes never leaving each other’s, in daylight, on State Street: “*Birthday sex* —”
A woman coming out of the bank on the corner with her deposit slip stops on the curb to watch.

In the turn lane beside them a silver Jetta has its windows down. In the passenger seat a college girl in an SBCC sweatshirt has her iPhone up at arm’s length, laughing so hard it shakes, pointed at them. Jack sees the phone. Skye, mid-verse, waves the lime at the Jetta like the grand marshal of something and doesn’t drop a word.

Somewhere in the second verse he thinks, very clearly, *Danny would pay money for this*, and then Skye leans across the gearshift and sings the next line with her mouth at his ear, and he loses the thought, and doesn’t miss it.
The light is still red. The verse runs out, and the hook is coming back around, and she points the lime at him: his.

choices.text: *Stand up in your seat for the hook.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you stood up in the Saab and sang it at her.
response: He stands up in the passenger seat with one hand on the windshield frame and gives the hook to State Street — to the bank and the palm and the shopping cart and the girl in the Jetta. Skye is laughing too hard to sing and conducts him anyway, with the lime, from below.
The light goes green with Jack still standing. She floors it, and he sits down hard in the leather with the song still going, laughing, his hand still up in the air where the windshield was.

choices.key: At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you did the high part — badly, at her, at the top of your lungs.
response: The falsetto, which he does not have, at full commitment, with his eyes shut and his hand on his heart for the anthem. Something comes out of him that the radio did not put there.

Skye stops singing. She stares at him the way you’d watch a dog parallel park, mouth open, the lime forgotten in her fist and her sunglasses sliding out of her hair, and every time she draws breath to say something he gives her another bar of it.
The light changes, and the car behind them honks, not unkindly, twice.

choices.text: *Sing it to her and nobody else.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you sang it to her and nobody else.
response: He turns all the way in his seat, one knee up on the leather, and sings it to her — every line he knows, straight at her, not loud now, the radio carrying the rest. It’s a ridiculous song, and he doesn’t sing it like one.
She stops conducting. The lime sits in her open hand on the gearshift. She takes the sunglasses down out of her hair and holds them, and doesn’t put them on.
The light changes. She doesn’t notice until the Jetta goes.

s05.slug: MONDAY · 9:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE LETTER
body: 412 with Theo out is a different country: the speaker dark, one desk lamp, one yellow circle on the blotter, and through the wall the clatter of Doug in Northrend, in long patient bursts, killing something large.

The Gospel at the twelve-ten was the man in the tombs, and Jack has been carrying him around since noon. A man with a regiment inside him, sitting at Jesus’s feet clothed and in his right mind, begging to be taken along in the boat, and told no: go home to your family and tell them. Danny’s review of the passage, delivered at eleven from the third pew at St. Brigid’s in a whisper that reached the sanctuary, was the pigs: two thousand of them, over a cliff, and somebody owed a farmer.

Letters to Trumbull have a grammar, and Jack could recite it like the Baltimore Catechism: no staples, no stickers, no perfume, no crayon, no cardstock, no clippings, nothing that could have been soaked in anything. Every page also has a second reader, a corrections officer at a table in Leavittsburg with a rubber stamp and a cup of coffee, whom Danny refers to in his own letters only as the State of Ohio, as in *the State of Ohio would like you to know it enjoyed your description of kelp.* So Jack writes for two readers, and it turns out to be the best thing that ever happened to his prose. Nothing in it can be wet. Everything in it is a fact or a joke, and a joke will carry a fact past the State of Ohio without being searched.

The card went Friday, in a smaller envelope inside Gina’s, with the number on the front. This is the letter, and it can be late. He uncaps the pen. Delgado stationery, cream, with the seal on it; block capitals, because that is how Danny writes to him, and a letter ought to answer in the language it was sent in. There is one sentence near the bottom that he writes twice. He draws three hard strokes through the first, and writes it again directly underneath, the same words in the same capitals, and leaves it there.

body.title: A letter, Delgado Hall stationery
body.text:
DAN —
HAPPY BIRTHDAY. 23. CANDLEMAS, WHICH NONNA SAYS MAKES YOU HOLY BY ACCIDENT.
THERE’S A BOX COMING FROM A STORE ON STATE STREET, BECAUSE THE CO’S LIKE IT BETTER FROM A STORE. A GIRL PICKED IT. SHE HAS OPINIONS ABOUT THE GRANDMOTHER. YOU’LL SEE.
THE SAINTS ARE IN IT. POP’S FOR THEM. HE SAYS NOBODY SHOULD HAVE TO WAIT LIKE US. LET HIM.
NONNA SAYS MARIA CATERINA NINE TIMES A DAY. SHE’S LEARNING IT FOR THE ROSARY.
YOU ASKED ME SOMETHING AT CHRISTMAS. I THINK I’VE GOT IT.
— PROFESSOR (J.)

body: He had *Skye* in the third line and took it out. Danny has her name already, by way of Gina, who forwards names like a switchboard, and the State of Ohio can do without.

The envelope is a glossy one from the bookstore’s ten-pack, and the pen skips on it. DANIEL COSTIGAN, and the number, A555218, which he knows the way he knows his birthday; TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION; LEAVITTSBURG, OHIO 44430. Every letter goes down in a small bead of ink that he drags along with the side of his hand, and when he rubs his face with that hand, because it is ten to ten and he has been up since a window on Del Playa went gold, the ink goes where the hand goes.
It wants a stamp, and sealing, and a place to be finished. The Fishbowl is lit downstairs and the hall up here is going quiet, and he can have either.

choices.text: Take it down to the Fishbowl.
response: He wants people around him and doesn’t say so. The Fishbowl is lit.
He stays at the desk with the window open and the hall going quiet.

s05a.slug: MONDAY · 11:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — TWO LEGAL PADS

body.text: Coming back up from the Fishbowl with the stamped envelope, Jack passes the lounge at the end of the fourth floor, and the door is open.
body.else: On his way down the hall to the stairs with the stamped envelope, Jack passes the lounge, and the door is open.

body: The television is dark and the vending machine is humming to itself. Two yellow legal pads lie side by side on the coffee table, each written over in a different hand, one spiky and slanting, one round, with circles over its *i*’s. On the carpet in front of them kneel Theo, in shirtsleeves, and Laney, in a Pi Lam sweatshirt and plaid pajama pants, with a pencil holding up her hair, each with one finger moving down one page, in time, line by line, like two people proofreading.
“…they can’t *both* be…” Laney is saying.
“…same night, Laney. Same *phone* —”
“Don’t you *Laney* me in that voice, Theodore. I’m working.”
Laney’s pad is face down before Jack has finished stopping. Theo’s follows half a second behind, with more grace and less speed.
“Wedding seating chart,” Theo says. “Hypothetical. Round tables, eight to a table. Nobody is speaking to the bride’s aunt.”
“The aunt,” Laney says, “has been through a great deal. And the groom’s people are Methodists, so they go by the exits, and near a pie.”
“Whose wedding?” Jack says.
“Hypothetical people,” says Laney. “They’re very happy.”

“They are *not* happy,” says Theo. “Their families have met. We’ve put the bride’s father by the open bar, which is the Christian thing, and the best man at the children’s table for reasons of national security.”

body.text:
“I thought it was a study group,” Jack says.

“The wedding is for the study group,” Theo says, without a flicker. “It’s a very large study.”

body: “You have ink on your face, Costigan,” Theo adds, changing the subject at once and with visible relief.

Laney gets up off the carpet. She has been cold to Jack for a month in a way that has rules, civil, exact, a *good morning* delivered at the right interval and a *Jack* with nothing on it, and now she crosses the room in her socks and looks at the side of his face. “Hold still.”
“I’m holding.”

“You are doing the opposite of holding.” She licks her thumb, there is no other way to say it, and takes something off his cheekbone in three brisk strokes, like a pageant mother going after lipstick on a front tooth. It is the first time Laney has touched him since she flattened his collar on the way to the dish return last week, and this time it is with saliva. She turns the thumb to the lamp. It is black at the tip. “Ink,” she says, and wipes it on Theo’s sleeve, and Theo says “*Hey*,” and she is already walking back to the carpet. “Night, sugar.”
He stays in the doorway long enough to see that the pads are going to stay face down for as long as he does, and goes. In 412 the envelope goes against the lamp, to ride down with him in the morning.

Theo comes in at twenty to twelve without the legal pad, and gets into bed in his shirt and trousers, and the room is dark but for the stairwell light under the door. Jack lies on top of the blanket and finds Hollis on the nightstand by the shape of the teacup.
“What are you doing the week of the seventh?” Theo says, to the ceiling.
“Working.”
“Hm.”
“Why?”
“No reason. Seven is a number your people like. Sacraments, sorrows, deadly sins. I’m a student of the form.”
Through the wall Doug’s tauren dies, loudly, and Doug says so.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again.

s05f.slug: MONDAY · 10:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: At ten the Fishbowl’s glass wall has stopped being a window and become a mirror, so that Jack, coming down the corridor with an envelope, meets a boy in a Carhartt coming toward him with an envelope, and the two of them reach the door together and have to let each other in.

Margot has the long table, with a mug of tea sweating on her notebook and, between her knuckles, a clove cigarette she is not permitted to light indoors, going end over end like a drum major’s baton. Doug has the near end, a laptop and a Hot Pocket whose second half is cooling in its sleeve. Kevin sits across from him with the orgo text open, a highlighter behind his ear, his BlackBerry face down on his notes. Over the vending alcove the television plays a panel of men in ties in total silence, under a crawl that says $3.8 TRILLION, and then THREE-YEAR FREEZE, and then a basketball score. The room is not watching it.

“Six,” Margot says, as Jack sits, as though they were in the middle of the sentence. “Six versions of Wednesday are now in circulation in this building. The sixth arrived this afternoon from the Classics department, which has given it a chorus.”
“A chorus.”
“Strophe, antistrophe. I’m told the dog has the best lines.”
“Read me one.”

“I don’t distribute primary sources.” She tips the clove at him. “You’d start correcting them, Costigan, and then they’d be yours. I will tell you that every version has two principals and a dog, and that where they differ is in whom the dog likes.”
“The dog likes everyone. The dog is deaf.”
“That,” Margot says, “is the first accurate sentence anyone has contributed in a week, and I resent that it came from a participant.”
Doug raises a hand from his Hot Pocket. “The one where the dog bit Costigan is mine.”
“It has acquired a limp,” Margot says.
“It’s *evolved*. He got bit at the *table*.”
“The dog was nowhere near the table.”
“Dude,” Doug says, with the patience of the wronged, “that’s what the dog would *say*.”

Jack lays the envelope on the table. It faces Kevin, upside down, in capitals: TRUMBULL, and the number. Kevin’s eyes stop on TRUMBULL for half a beat, and then the highlighter starts moving again. Jack pats his pockets for the stamps Ma packed in August and remembers where they are, which is on his desk, upstairs, doing nothing. Kevin’s hand goes to his back pocket. He produces a single stamp in a glassine sleeve out of a wallet that has a place for everything, and slides it across the laminate, without looking up.
“Thanks, Kev.”

“Don’t thank me,” Kevin tells the page. “It’s the first thing anybody’s needed from me tonight that I could actually supply.” He underlines something. “Clare’s grandfather’s violin is Czech, by the way. A hundred years old, and in better tune than the nine-thirty band, which I say with love, because I’m in it.”
The stamp takes two tries on the glossy paper. Jack licks the flap. It tastes like the bookstore’s glue and a little like the pen.
“Mailing something to Ohio by hand,” Margot says, to the clove. “You’re a nineteenth-century man, Costigan.”
“Eighteen.”
“Till March. I have the date.”

He takes the stairs up with the envelope in his coat and Theo’s Penguin in the other pocket, and on the fourth-floor landing the lounge light is on, laying a yellow rectangle across the carpet as far as the stairwell door.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them.

body: By ten the hall has gone the way Delgado goes on a Monday, doors shutting in order from the elevator end, until all that’s left of the floor is Doug’s keyboard through the wall and the window Jack has propped four inches to let in the cold and the eucalyptus, in that order. At half past, Priya makes her rounds, one knock per door and the same sentence in the same key, *quiet hours are not suggestions*, and to 412, whose door is open, she says it twice and adds, to the room at large, “I’m going to need that door to commit.”

On the pillow the Penguin lies face down at the goose. The RAZR sits beside the lamp, quiet; Skye has lines to run for a tape she won’t name yet, and he believes her. He reads the letter over once and changes nothing. Then he goes through the duffel under the bed for a stamp and finds the book Ma packed in August, in the front pocket, with a Post-it on it in her St. Brigid’s secretary’s hand that says LETTERS. She packed a book of twenty. There are four left. Ma, who can audit a household by its stamps, will want to know who got the other sixteen, and the answer, mostly, is Danny.

At twenty to eleven Theo comes in, in shirtsleeves, the blazer over his arm and the pin clipped to the lapel, and stops at the sight of the envelope on the blotter. He reads the address from where he stands. “Is it tomorrow?”
“Tomorrow.”
“Twenty-three.” He considers it. “Tell the man the hat is holding up. It survived pledge week with its dignity, which is more than I can say for the Browns’ secondary.”
“I’ll tell him.”

Theo crosses to his desk, opens the drawer, and takes out a yellow legal pad written over from margin to margin, and holds it against his chest, face in. “Study group,” he says. “Laney’s. Statistics. There’s a thermos, and a professor’s old midterm.”
“You’ve never been in a study group.”
“I’m diversifying.” He is gone before the drawer has finished sliding shut.

With Theo out the room goes back to itself. Rosie’s Christmas drawing has slipped on its tack again, Jack very tall beside a crab the size of a dog and a tree with a star bigger than either of them, and he puts it straight with his thumb. Over his narrow bed the crucifix. Over Theo’s desk the princes Rosie drew him, taped up at Christmas and defended ever since against all comers; in the frame of Theo’s mirror, Nonna’s twenty. On the sill the porch on Glenwood in a drugstore print, with Ma’s thumb in one corner. On the nightstand, in his teacup, Hollis, at rest.
He stamps the envelope with Ma’s stamp, and it goes on crooked, and he lets it. Her book of twenty is down to three. Through the wall Doug kills the large thing a second time, with feeling.
At a quarter past eleven he turns off the lamp, picks the envelope up off the blotter, and goes out.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 7:15 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE NEWS FEED
body: The window in 412 faces the ridge, and at a quarter past seven on Candlemas the ridge still has the sun, so the only light in the room is the MacBook’s, laid up under Theo’s chin. He is standing at his desk in the wine-colored robe with a mug of tea going cold in one hand, reading, and he has not woken Jack to do it. On the other desk the envelope for Trumbull leans against the lamp, waiting for a mailbox.
The bedsprings give Jack away. “Costigan,” Theo says, without turning. “Sit up. You’re being remembered in the prayers of the faithful.”
He clears his throat, and the voice comes down over him like a stole: the lector at the twelve-ten, slow, a little through the nose, every name given its full weight.

body: “For Thomas Hritz, of Youngstown, Ohio,” Theo reads, “who had it from a *Sweetwater* fan page, who had it from somebody’s cousin in Boardman, and who has discovered capital letters and does not intend to give them back.” Jack, sitting up, gives him nothing. “Lord, hear our prayer,” Theo answers for him, and scrolls.

body.name: Doug Pruitt
body.text: DUUUUDE

body: “For Douglas Pruitt, who was awake at twelve fifty-one and is presumably still a druid.” A chair rolls back on the far side of the cinderblock, and Doug’s voice comes through it, long and glad and nearly all vowel: “DUUUUUDE.” “Lord,” says Theo, “hear our prayer.”
“For Priya Raman, who has posted the quiet hours to a medium that has none.” He scrolls on without waiting for anybody.

He goes back to Tommy’s post and clicks through, turns the speaker down to a murmur, and steps aside so Jack can see. Thirty-eight seconds, shot out a passenger window from the next lane at a red light, the picture jumping, a girl laughing somewhere behind the phone. It swings, steadies, and there is a face Jack has only ever seen from the inside, mouth open at the top of its lungs and aimed at a girl in sunglasses, who is aiming right back. The hook comes thin and tinny out of the speaker. What Jack hears is her under it, half a beat early and dead certain. He has never caught himself in a mirror making that face.

“Eleven thousand,” Theo says, in his own voice. “Before seven.” He lets the video run on into its sidebar of other people’s cats. “It isn’t the eleven thousand that worries me, Costigan. It’s that each of them has a mother, a pastor, and a cousin in Youngstown.”
“Youngstown’s a big town.”

“Youngstown is a prayer chain with a zip code.” He drags the picture back three seconds and lets it play again, mute. “Now watch her. Photographed professionally since before either of us could shave, and she is the only person in this frame who knows where the camera is, and she doesn’t look at it. I have seen that woman take a forkful of salad at a better angle than most people get married.”
Jack has seen her check the angle on a taco. On the screen she sings at him, and the lens is somebody else’s problem.

body: “Antiphonal,” Theo reads, and the voice is gone; it simply isn’t there. “Two choirs across an aisle, each answering the other. She took the verse and you took the hook.” He looks at the screen. “Margot is right, which I find upsetting before breakfast.”

He scrolls to the next one, a name from Newman, and his mouth opens for the voice and the voice doesn’t come. He reads the rest to himself. The lid of the MacBook goes down to a crack of light, and his finger stays on it.
“You look happy,” Theo says.
“I am.”
“So the footage suggests.” He takes the towel off its hook and the caddy off the doorknob. “I’m going to stand under hot water until I’m a better man. Expect me at noon.”
The RAZR has been collecting on Jack’s desk since before dawn.
