body: He can see the third one entire: the laptop on the oilcloth beside the Folgers can, Nonna in her housedress at the kitchen table, both hands coming together for a girl in a car. The last two came in from Ursuline, where a phone in homeroom is a detention, and Gina has weighed the price and paid it. He reads the last one twice. On the day Danny turns twenty-three, the news from Jack Costigan is that he sang in a car.
It rings in his hand before he can answer a single one. The outside screen says ST BRIGID SCH.
“Happy Candlemas,” Ma says. She has the office voice on, all edges. “Your brother is twenty-three.”
“Ma, I —”

“I have four minutes and a bell, so I’m not asking if you ate.” Behind her a copier thunks, and a small voice says *Mrs. Costigan* in the tone of the gravely ill. “Wait, Kyle. Gina had it at breakfast, Jackie, because Gina can’t keep a thing off a screen. By the time I got to my desk Ryan Pallante had shown his mother, and Rita had shown Father Dom’s secretary, and Father Dom’s secretary had shown *Father Dom*, who asked me at the copier whether you were eating.”
“What did you tell him?”

“That you’re a growing boy. Then his secretary showed it to me, with the sound off, in front of the copier. Everybody knows what the song’s called. I’m not going to say the name of it. It’s your brother’s birthday.”

“Danny called the house at seven, before I left. I told him there’s a video of a song and I’m not saying which. He said, *Ma, say it.* I said, *Daniel, it’s your birthday.* He says he’ll try you this afternoon, if they give him the phone. Pick up.”
“I will.”
From the far side of the office, high and old and delighted: “*Cassidy canta!*”

“Mamma, *sit*.” The phone muffles and comes back. “She came in with me for the candles, and they gave her a chair, and she’s using it as a stage. Your father watched it in the garage on Nonna’s laptop, Jackie; Gina carried it out to him. Three times. I counted through the door. He came in the kitchen and said, *Kid can’t hold a note. Never could*, and went back out. And your brother can’t have a cake, they won’t allow it. I made the lemon one last night anyway. Your father had the first piece standing up at the counter and called it quality control.”

body.text: “And Rita Pallante printed a still of it. It’s on her refrigerator, under St. Joseph, right next to your *Yes*. She called to tell me. I thanked her for her concern.”
“She knelt Sunday and sang that Monday. That girl’s a whole liturgical year.”

body: “We bless the candles at eleven,” Ma says, in the manner of a woman reading her own sentence. “The children may not light them, by order of the fire marshal, so it will be two hundred unlit candles and Kyle, who wants to know why.” A bell starts somewhere on her end and is overruled by a door. “Jackie. I watched it with the sound off. Were you *happy*?”

“Yes, Ma.” He says it before she has finished the word. Over the ridge the sun clears the oaks at last, and 412 goes from the laptop’s blue to just a room. Down on the quad the sprinklers come on in a line, one head at a time, and throw their first arcs against the light.
“Good.” A drawer slams on her end. “Then sing something else next time.”

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good. Candlemas morning, from the school office between bells: my brother’s twenty-three, and Father Dom’s secretary has seen the video. She won’t say the name of the song. Pop says I can’t hold a note. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. Sing something else next time.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first. Monday she found me on a celebrity blog before I did, and knew Danny’s jacket. A man from Mahoning County called Danny a name in the comments; she reported him, answered him, and called him one back — a Catholic one. She’s making Danny a card for Candlemas. Tuesday Ashley Vrabel showed her the picture in chem. Capitals. Wednesday, at three in the morning her time: Nonna wants a baptism name, for the rosary. Friday she was lowercase again: *mary catherine?????* Nonna said it nine times at breakfast and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. My Candlemas card for Danny goes in her envelope Monday. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday. She’s telling him in person. Tuesday, six in the morning her time, on Nonna’s computer: JACK. WHAT DID YOU DO. Then the whole homeroom. DANNYS BIRTHDAY JACK.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.* Thursday night I sent Gina the name: Mary Catherine. At breakfast Nonna said *Maria Caterina* nine times, and cried the good kind, and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. Candlemas she went to the school office with Ma for the candles, and heard her on the phone with me. *Cassidy canta!*

choices.text: “It was Skye’s idea. I sang the loud part.”
choices.key: On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her it was Skye’s idea and you sang the loud part.
response: “That’s not the defense you think it is,” Ma says. Across the office Nonna has the last word, delighted: “*Brava!*” “Mamma, *no*.”
The bell goes, the electric kind, right through the receiver. “Eat something,” Ma says over it, and the line is gone.

choices.key: On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her to tell Nonna that Cassidy’s got range.
response: Ma tells her. Word for word, across the office, to the room. Nonna’s laugh comes down the line like a kettle coming to the boil, and goes on coming.
“I’m hanging up, Jackie,” Ma says. “I have a school.”

choices.key: On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her to tell Danny it was for him.
response: “I will *not*,” Ma says. Her hand goes over the receiver, and through it, muffled and scandalized, comes the room: “Mamma, he says it was *for* Danny.”
Nonna answers with something in dialect, of which Jack gets a word and Ma gets all of it. “*Mamma!*” And the line goes.

s06a.slug: TUESDAY · 12:20 PM · MORRO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Oceanography 1 is two hundred people in raked seats in Morro 1100, and by eleven on Tuesday it’s safe to assume all of them have seen it. A kid in row nine hums the hook at them as they come down the side aisle, falsetto included, and three rows laugh. Fenner lets it go until he has the refraction diagram up — a long swell out of the northwest in yellow chalk, bending around a headland — and then he turns from the board with the chalk still up, finds them in the back row under the exit sign, and says, “Pair forty-one, *please*,” and the room loses it. Jack puts his forehead down on the fold-out desk. Beside him Skye uncaps a pen and copies the diagram into the margin of her notes, crest by crest, each one bending a little more than the last as it feels the bottom, and doesn’t look up until she has the final wave wrapped around the Point.

“It slows down in the shallow part,” she says, when he lifts his head. “So it turns toward it. Everything bends toward the shallow end.” She underlines it. “Fenner thinks that’s oceanography. It’s the internet.”

Morro lets out down its front steps into a hard, clean noon: backpacks, a longboard under somebody’s arm, a girl walking and eating an apple. Skye stops on the fourth step with her sunglasses in her hand and lets the class go around her like she’s a rock in a creek.
On the walk over from Delgado he gave her Ma’s call — Ryan Pallante and his mother and Father Dom’s secretary — and she made him do Rita twice. Now it’s her turn.

“Corinne called at six,” she says. “Debbie called at six-oh-four. Debbie doesn’t call. Debbie has people for calling.” She holds her iPhone up at him: a gossip site he’s never heard of, pink banner, a still of the two of them at the light with her mouth wide open on a note. *SWEETWATER’S GOOD GIRL GONE WILD?* “With a question mark. The question mark is working very hard.” She puts the phone against her chest. “The network wants to know if Cassidy is still Cassidy. They’re using the word *brand*. In a sentence. About me.”

“Cassidy,” she says, “would have sung a hymn at that light. In harmony. And the light would’ve turned green out of respect.” She hooks a finger through his belt loop to keep him on her step while a pack of lacrosse players goes by in their pinnies. “I’m not Cassidy. Cassidy is four writers and a lighting guy. I just stand where they put the tape.”
“What’s Corinne saying?”

“Corinne’s saying it’s an *unauthorized clip*.” She does it in Corinne’s mouth, every consonant filed. “She said it to me four times so I’d learn it. Like somebody bootlegged a concert.” The sunglasses go on. “Then she asked me if I regretted it, and I said I’d get back to her.”
She looks out past the bike racks at the lagoon, bright and still, a couple of pelicans standing around on the sandbar with nothing to do.
“There are hundreds of hours of me on tape, Jack. Hours. If the building was on fire I’d go back in for those thirty-eight seconds.”
He looks at her. She posts everything — the taco photo, a sunset at the Rincon, a menu she disagrees with — and this morning there is nothing about it on her page at all.
“You didn’t put it up.”

“Your mother’s secretary’s priest has seen it, Jack.” She has the chain slightly wrong, and it doesn’t slow her down. “I’m not putting it on a plate for them. Some girl in a Jetta put it up without asking. That’s on her. I don’t do that to you on purpose.” She turns the iPhone around. “This, I did on purpose.”

The kid from row nine comes down the steps past them, walking backward so he can point. “Forty-one!” Then, still backing: “Wait. Are you the guy from the professor’s house? Which one were you — the one who lied, or the one who got lied about?”
Jack looks at him until the kid remembers he has somewhere to be.

The kid takes the look with him down the steps. Skye watches him go and says, “Debbie wants me to do a sit-down with a magazine about my *journey*,” and goes on with Debbie, and doesn’t ask what the kid meant.
Jack watches her talk. Her mother’s six-oh-four. A network that bought a nice girl and wants her back. A word like *brand* said about her over breakfast. He did that, at a red light, with a lime.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Skye, till May. No trades. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere. Sunday: the Point open again — breaking where it does. Saturday at the Point with Fenner’s form and a stopwatch, timing the sets. Skye called the surfers like the last hole of a golf tournament. Breaking where it does. Tuesday two hundred people had seen it. Fenner said Pair forty-one, *please*, and the room lost it. Skye was doing his refraction diagram in the margin.

journal.title: Corinne Waxman
journal.text: Corinne Waxman. Skye’s publicist. Answers the phone with her own name. Reads a BlackBerry the way other people read a room; uses a legal pad only when a lawyer might read it later. Ran my name in January. Tuesday she read the *Vindicator* off it, and asked me, kindly, what happened. Wrote down Danny’s number when Skye said it. Thursday: a fundraiser in the Palisades. It’s civic. Thursday she wanted the arrival picture on Skye’s page; she got tacos and a caption. She stopped typing for most of the argument. She says I was supposed to be furniture. The host’s office called her twice: Gil wants us both back in the spring. The taco picture is sweet, she says, and sweet isn’t a strategy. Tuesday she called Skye at six. The clip is unauthorized, she says. Skye wrote on my wall anyway.

s06b.slug: TUESDAY · 2:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — THE HEARING
body: The fourth-floor lounge at five past two has the flat high light that shows what the carpet has been through. The television bolted in the corner is running the morning’s hearing again, the Senate Armed Services Committee, a man in a gray suit at one end of a long table and a man in Navy blues at the other, and a crawl under them with three letters in it. On the whiteboard somebody has written HAPPY CANDLEMAS over Sunday’s raid schedule in green marker and drawn a candle with a face. Jack is passing through with half a Commons sandwich in a napkin, and he stops in the doorway.

Kevin is on the arm of the couch with the orgo text open on his knee and the cap still on his highlighter. Yusuf has the other arm and a statics problem set he is not working. On the screen an anchor with a lacquered voice is saying that Admiral Mullen, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, told the senators that allowing gays and lesbians to serve openly “would be the right thing to do,” and that Senator McCain said he was deeply disappointed.
“Since when do you watch the news?” Jack says.

“Since it got an admiral.” Kevin doesn’t take his eyes off the screen. “I’m a sucker for a hat.” His eyes go to the napkin in Jack’s hand. “That sandwich has been out of the cooler since Sunday. I’m not saying it’s a pathogen with mayonnaise. I’m saying I’d want it looked at.”
He finds the remote on the cushion and turns the volume up one notch as the anchor reaches the admiral, and then, as she finishes, down again.
“He’s an admiral,” Kevin says. Jack takes it for rank. Kevin salutes crossing guards.
“They’ll argue about it for a year,” Yusuf says, to his problem set. “My brother says nobody in his unit asked.”
“How is Tariq?” Jack says.
“Further up the stairs every Sunday. He rates the handrails.”

Kevin mutes the set and uncaps the highlighter at last. “Clare asked me last night,” he says, “after band, over the music stands, which of you was right at Hale’s. I told her I didn’t have the information. She said that was a very Kevin answer. I think it was a compliment.”
“It was.”

“I’m logging it as one, pending review.” He lays a yellow stripe across a paragraph on the Krebs cycle, apparently at random. “Then she made me hold her music stand while she thought about it. Eleven minutes. She says that’s how she knows I’m loyal.”

body.text:
“Is today your brother’s?” Kevin asks. He saw the envelope last night, upside down on the Fishbowl table, and asked nothing then.

“Twenty-three.”
body.else: Jack checks the RAZR, finds nothing, and says it to the room. “It’s my brother’s birthday. He’s calling this afternoon, if they let him.”

body: Kevin turns from the screen for the first time since the doorway. “Is he okay?”
“He’s calling.” It is the answer Jack has.

Kevin nods and turns a page he hasn’t read. On the screen the senator is disappointed again, at greater length, and Yusuf’s pencil comes to rest on the problem set. Jack drops the sandwich in the bin by the stairs, on the strength of the medical opinion, and takes the stairs down toward Del Playa.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING
body: The swing hangs at Sol’s again, the old driftwood seat on new galvanized chain that still creaks like a pair of new shoes whenever anybody shifts. Below the bluff the surf is big and left over from some storm up by Alaska, and the sun has started down the back half of the afternoon toward the Point. Skye has her knees up inside his flannel and her bare feet on the front edge of the seat. Her iPhone is face down on the boards where she dropped it, and it has been buzzing since he sat down — Corinne, every couple of minutes, the phone walking itself across the wood toward the steps until Skye puts out a heel and shoves it back under the swing, where it goes on buzzing against the boards.

The RAZR goes off on his knee. On the little outside screen, a long 330 number he has never saved and would know in his sleep. 3:40 here, 6:40 in Leavittsburg: after count, after chow, his brother’s turn at the wall.

He opens it. The recording comes on loud enough for the porch. “This is a prepaid call from —” and into the gap, fast, his brother’s own voice: “Danny.” “— an inmate at Trumbull Correctional Institution. This call is subject to monitoring and recording. To accept, press one.”
Jack presses one.
“Professor.”
“Happy birthday, Dan.”

“This is recorded, so everybody keep it clean,” Danny says. “Hi, State of Ohio.” Behind him, a hallway: a TV turned up for a room, a door that bangs on a spring. “Twenty-three. Old enough to know better. Ain’t stopped me yet. Called the house this morning, caught Ma with her coat on, so this one’s yours. Two calls. I’m living large.” A breath. “Gina’s envelope ain’t come. She says there’s two cards in it and one’s got a candle on it, and she won’t say whose. Late’s a Costigan tradition.”
“Pop’s never been on time to anything but a shift.”
Danny laughs, the short one. “He was early to those. Twenty-six years, he was early.”

body.text: “Your girl’s letter came. In capitals. Nobody writes me in capitals but my sister and the State of Ohio.” Beside him Skye puts both hands over her mouth.
body.else: “Your girl says she wrote. I’m holding her to it.” Beside him Skye puts a hand over her eyes.

body.text: Before Danny can get to the song, Jack says it. “It was for you, Dan.” “Ma ain’t gonna tell me that,” Danny says. “Ma’s gonna take that to her grave and then tell St. Peter.”

body: “So Ma wouldn’t say the name of it,” Danny says. “On my *birthday*, Professor. She said there’s a video and a song she won’t say, and then she said happy birthday like she was reading it off a sympathy card. What’d you *sing*?”

body.text: “I stood up in the car,” Jack says, which isn’t the question.
“I did the high part,” Jack says, which isn’t the question.
“I sang it at her,” Jack says, which isn’t the question.

body: Skye has been listening with her chin on her knees. Now she unfolds one arm out of the flannel and holds out her hand to him and crooks her fingers twice. “Give me him.”
He gives her him. She hits the speaker key like she’s done it on a RAZR all her life and sets the phone on her knee, face up. “I want you to hear this,” she tells Jack.
“Hello?” says Trumbull, suspicious.
“Danny,” she says. “Happy birthday. It’s Skye.”
“So you’re the one,” Danny says, warm as anything, out of Leavittsburg. “What’d you lose the bet for?”
“Danny. Danny.” She puts a hand on her heart. “There was no bet. There was an *operation*.”
And she tells him the trick.

It starts in October, with a recall notice under her wiper: General Motors letterhead, very official, very creased. Her Saab, which is a GM car — “look it up, Danny, he made me look it up” — “It’s a GM car,” Danny agrees — has a defect in what the notice calls the emotional transmission, and the only man in California certified to repair it is a specialist from Lordstown. Enter Jack, in coveralls, with his name sewn over the pocket. “What name?” Danny says. “*Jack*. In cursive. He did it himself. Badly.”

He needed a man on the inside, so he bribed his roommate with a Browns hat. “So *that’s* where the hat came from,” Danny says. “I thought the rich one just had taste.” “The *rich* one,” Skye says, delighted. “Is that what you call him? I call him Ted. Yours is so much better.” Ted, she explains, would sell her to a circus for a hat; Ted has a hat problem; Ted got her address.

There is a woman at a diner on the harbor who rates men by pie. So Jack’s grandmother mailed a Calabrese love spell out to California in a coffee can, and it went into the crust. “It’s in the *crust*, Danny. That’s why he’s lattice-top.” “What’s lattice-top?” “Pretty on top. Everything’s leaking underneath.” “That’s him,” Danny says. “That’s him *exactly*.”

After that he came to her door as a Bible salesman, in a hat, with a sample case, and the Bible was hollow — “like in the story, Danny, he reads the stories, he knew *exactly* what he was doing” — and inside the hollow Bible was —
“Ma’am,” Danny says, “the State of Ohio is *listening*.”
“— a coupon,” Skye says. “For pie.”

That’s where Danny goes. It’s the big one, the laugh Jack gets maybe once a visit, that starts somewhere under Danny’s ribs and takes all the air out of him on the way up, and it comes out of the little speaker on her knee so loud she flinches and the chain creaks. Somewhere behind it a man’s voice, bored and far off, says *Costigan, keep it down.* Danny, with the phone away from his mouth: “Sorry, sir — family news.”

Skye doesn’t wait for him. There was an actor hired to play a priest and tell her it was God’s will — “I know actors, Danny, the man couldn’t kneel, he went down like a card table” — and a permission slip, signed by the Pope, in green ink. “Which Pope?” “The current one, Danny, I’m not an *animal*.” And there was the book. Jack had operatives plant a paperback Flannery O’Connor in a den in Montecito, open to the grandmother, and wait in the shrubbery for her to sit down beside it.
“He did that to a girl in eighth grade,” Danny says, wheezing, “with a Pontiac.”
“*Which* girl.”
“I’ll send you a list.”

Somewhere around the Pope she loses the thread of her own sentence, and instead of going back for it she laughs and lets it go, and Danny, who never knew there was a thread, laughs harder. Her heels push the swing off the boards and it comes back on its own, and she doesn’t put a hand out to catch it. When he tops her with the Pontiac she points at the phone, delighted, at a man in Leavittsburg who can’t see her do it. Under the swing Corinne walks across the boards again, and Skye’s bare heel stays up in the air, keeping time. Jack has watched her be funny all winter. This is the first time he has watched her get lost in it.
“And you want to know *why*, Danny?” she says. “The coveralls. The hat. The *Pope*.”
“Why.”
“He was out of stamps. He needed somebody else to write you.”
Jack puts his face in his hands. In Leavittsburg his brother makes a noise like a man falling down a flight of stairs on purpose.
It takes Danny some time to come back. When he does he is wheezing, and his voice is smaller and nearer the phone. “Okay. Okay.” A breath that rattles. “What’d he really do.”
Skye stops the swing with her heel.

“The Friday before Thanksgiving,” she says. “A house in Montecito. A boy named Wyatt Halloran whose parents were in London. Half the people there I went to middle school with, and I didn’t want one of them to see me alone. I was in the window seat in the den, because it was the one place in that house nobody could stand behind me. I had a paperback of *A Good Man Is Hard to Find* and a Sharpie, because I was reading for a preacher’s daughter who forgives a boy in the rain, and I’d decided the grandmother was a liar. I wrote LIAR in the margin next to her. Four times. Bigger every time.”
She pulls the flannel tighter over her knees.
“I had one boot on, Danny. I was leaving.”
Jack’s hand on the chain stops.

“And this guy comes across the room. Borrowed shirt — it was Ted’s, I didn’t know that yet. He didn’t know who I was. He didn’t care who I was. He crossed the den by himself to tell me I had the grandmother backwards. So I argued, and he argued back, and he was good, and he was annoying, and I asked him the thing I couldn’t figure out — at the end, when she reaches out and touches the man with the gun, what does she *want*? Because everybody in every scene wants something. That’s the job.” She stops, and starts again. “And he said, ‘Nothing. That’s the point. For one second she doesn’t want anything from anybody. That’s what grace looks like from the outside. And he can’t stand it.’”
The surf comes in under the bluff and goes out.

“I had PLAY IT AS A CON at the bottom of the page,” she says. “And I crossed out CON. In my own margin. I’ve never crossed out a note in my life, Danny. Notes are how I get paid.” “Then I drove him up the coast to a beach of mine and dared him into the Pacific in his clothes, and he emptied his pockets onto my boots and walked into the Pacific in his jeans one step at a time like it was a procession, and I called him Coat check, and he’s been Coat check since. And we talked till it got gray.”

“You want to know when I decided to kiss him? Around the grandmother’s hand on the Misfit’s shoulder. Two and a half hours before I asked. And then when I finally asked, he didn’t let me finish.” She breathes out. “I still have the book. It’s on my nightstand. CON’s still crossed out.”
Jack has woken up beside that nightstand and never once read the spine on it.
“That’s what he did,” Skye says, very quietly. “He didn’t want anything from me. All night. He just wanted me to be right about the grandmother.”
The chain is cold under his hand.
