s07a.slug: TUESDAY · 3:53 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING

body.text: Her hand is in his on the seat, warm and tight, and on the phone, nothing.
She’s still looking at him, and on the phone, nothing.
“State facility,” she repeats, to herself, and on the phone, nothing.
Her last sentence goes out over the porch rail toward the water, and on the phone, nothing.

body: Just the hiss of the line, and a long way behind it the TV for somebody else’s room and a door banging on its spring. It goes on long enough that Jack leans to look at the screen to see if the call has dropped. The seconds are still counting.
Danny coughs. It goes on too long for a cough.
“Lady,” he says, when he has it back down, “I’m in *prison*. You can’t do that to me in *here*.”
Skye laughs, and it comes out wet, and she wipes under one eye with the cuff of the flannel.
“*Professor*,” Danny says.
Just that.
The recording cuts in over it, the same flat woman. “You have one minute remaining.”
Skye picks the RAZR up off her knee with both hands and holds it close. “Call me,” she says into it. “Call *us*. I’ll be the one who answers.”

body.text: “Yeah. Yeah, I’ll call.” A breath. “You keep that phone charged, Mary Catherine.”
body.else: “Yeah. Yeah, I’ll call. You keep that phone charged.”

body.text: At the name she shuts her eyes, and keeps them shut till she has the phone back on her knee.

body: She puts it in Jack’s hand, still on speaker, and stays against his shoulder, close enough to hear the line breathing. He leans down to it.
“She’s the one I can tell the truth to.”
“Yeah, I can tell, Professor. You’re not subtle. I’m still going with the trick though, easier to wrap my brain around that one.”

The line clicks. On the screen the call timer stops, and then it says CALL ENDED, and then it’s only the time. After that it’s the porch: the surf under the bluff, a car going by slow on Del Playa with its windows down, the new chains.
Jack sits with the dead phone open in his hand. The swing goes on moving a little by itself, the way it does after somebody gets off it, except nobody has.
Skye takes the RAZR out of his hand, folds it shut, and gives it back to him.
“He laughs like you,” she says. “When you forget to be careful.”
Under the swing the iPhone starts up against the boards again. She lets it go three buzzes before she reaches down for it, turns it over, and answers it without looking at the name.
“Not now, Corinne. I’m at a birthday.”
She hangs up, drops it in the flannel’s front pocket, puts her feet to the boards, and pushes off, and they swing.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas, his twenty-third, he called from Trumbull and got Skye. Gina’s envelope hadn’t come — two cards in it, she says, and one with a candle. Skye’s letter came, in capitals. Ma wouldn’t tell him the name of the song. Skye told him how I tricked her — a long caper, a love spell in Gloria’s crust — and he laughed till they told him to keep it down. Family news, he said. Then she told him what really happened in Montecito, and he coughed for a while. She asked him to call again. I told him she’s the one I can tell the truth to. He said I’m not subtle. He’s still going with the trick.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 5:15 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — CANDLEMAS
s08.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Lumen ad revelationem gentium”
body: The sun is down behind the oaks, but the sky over them hasn’t got the news yet, a long bruised yellow going green at the top, and the olive-tree courtyard at St. Brendan’s is full of people holding candles that aren’t lit: Newman kids in hoodies, the weekday regulars, a nurse in scrubs and clogs straight off a shift. Joey Abruzzo has the basket at the gate and is telling everybody within a block that the paper drip guards ran out at the 12:10.

Skye’s candle is bare. She went upstairs after the call and came down in the gray cardigan, the sixty-eight-dollar one she bought for Mass, the flannel left on the swing, and now she holds the candle in front of her in both fists and studies the wick.
“What’s my motivation,” she says, low.
“Don’t set anybody’s hair on fire.”
“That’s a note. That’s not a motivation.”

Father Osei comes out the side door in white, a server behind him with a lit taper, and the flame goes out through the crowd wick to wick until the courtyard is full of small fire. He reads the blessing, short, and swings the aspergillum. The drops land cold on Jack’s cheek. Skye shuts her eyes and takes hers on the face like weather. A gust comes down off the ridge and takes a dozen flames at once, hers among them.
She turns to him without a word and tips her wick into his.

He holds still for it. Her face is lit from underneath, a loose piece of hair at her ear, her eyes crossed a little with the care she’s taking, her breath moving both flames. The wax smells like a sacristy. It takes. She doesn’t step back right away, and he wants her, here, with the holy water drying on his face, and there’s no use pretending otherwise to God, who has the better view. The woman on her other side holds out a dark wick, and Skye lights it, and the woman lights the next.

Past the fountain, Laney Price is holding her candle out at the full length of her arm, away from her hair, with the face of a woman defusing something. Lena is beside her, her own candle held close. Jack sees her across a courtyard of candles, one lit face in a crowd of them, and looks past her through the open doors to the altar. Two girls from Newman look from him to the fountain and back, and find something to do with their candles when he catches them.
“Let us go in peace,” Osei says, “to meet the Lord.”

*Lumen ad revelationem gentium*, the choir sings at the doors, and the line goes in under it, out of the dusk and up the aisle under the ship’s-hull ceiling, the blue glass gone black in the windows above a churchful of candles. Halfway up, a bead of wax runs down Skye’s candle and over her thumb. Her mouth tightens. She doesn’t move the thumb. By the pew it has cooled to a white cap on the knuckle.

Osei reads the Gospel himself: Mary and Joseph bringing the child up to the Temple with two turtledoves because they can’t afford the lamb, and old Simeon taking him in his arms. *A light for revelation to the Gentiles.* Then the prophetess, Anna, a widow till she was eighty-four, who never left the temple.
At *The Gospel of the Lord* Skye leans in to his ear. “Eighty-four,” she whispers. “She waited eighty-four years for an *entrance*.”
Jack has to look at his shoes until Osei starts to speak.

Osei closes the book. “Simeon waited his whole life to see one thing, and when they put it in his arms he did not say, *Now I will keep him*,” he says. “He asked to be let go. And to the mother he says, *and you yourself a sword will pierce* — and the light is for the Gentiles, which is to say for everybody, which is the hard part, because everybody includes the one you would not have invited.” He goes back to his chair.

Jack thinks of Ma at the Trumbull vending machines every other Sunday with a sandwich bag of quarters, and of *Professor* on the porch this afternoon with nothing after it. At the intentions he adds his own, straight. *Twenty-three today. He’s got a book coming late. Keep him till it gets there. Keep him after.*

At Communion Gus keeps the organ low and the pews empty forward one by one from the front. When it’s theirs, Jack doesn’t stand. Skye doesn’t get up to let him by. She turns her knees to let the row out past them, and while Jack is still working out what to do with his candle she takes it out of his hand and holds it with hers, one in each fist, his and the bare one with the wax on her thumb.
He kneels. She stays sitting beside him, straight-backed, holding them both.
He says the Act of Contrition slowly, the one he could say in his sleep, and slows down more at *firmly resolve*, and gets to the end of it.

The line coming back goes down the side aisle past the end of the pew, and with his head bowed he sees it from the knee down: a toddler’s light-up sneaker, a pair of wingtips, a candle held out at the full length of somebody’s arm though it’s been out since the Gospel. Beside it, a pair of flats slows at the end of the pew and stops, longer than the line has stopped. A hand settles on the back of Laney’s coat and steers her on into a pew farther down.
Jack keeps his head down. Beside him Skye gets both candles into one hand and puts the other on his back, high up, and keeps it there till he sits.
At the door Osei has a candle in his left hand and takes Jack’s with his right, and holds it a second longer than a handshake. His eyes are having a wonderful time.
“I saw your concert,” he says.
And nothing else. He lets go, sees Skye’s full hands, and gives her a little bow from the neck instead. She bows back exactly as far.

Becca Lindell is on the step below in a peacoat with her own candle. “Happy Candlemas, Jack,” she says. “Hi, Skye.” She looks at the wax on Skye’s thumb, slides the paper guard off her own candle, and fits it down over Skye’s until it sits against the knuckle. “There,” she says.
Mrs. Fitch is at the foot of the steps, collecting stubs in Joey’s empty basket. “Mr. Costigan,” she says. “Four people have asked me whether that was you. I told them I was sure it was not.”
Skye presses her lips together until they go white and holds them that way to the bottom of the steps.

Under the olive trees people are carrying their candles off to the lot, the flames out, the wax still soft. Skye hands Jack back his candle. She looks at the two of them, his and hers, Becca’s guard very white on hers.
“I held those through the good part,” she says. “I want that in the credits.”

response: He holds his out to her. She looks at it, and at him, and takes it, and gives him hers straight back.
“Trade,” she says. “Then we’ve both got one the other one held.”
He puts hers in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, Becca’s guard and all. She carries his across the lot to the Saab and lays it on the dash like a corsage, and tells it to stay.
“For Nonna,” he says. He’ll tell her about it on the phone: candles lit outdoors in February under olive trees, a priest from Ghana with holy water, a gust. You can’t mail fire.
Skye nods like that’s obviously correct, and carries hers down the walk to the lot in both hands, like it’s still lit.

s09.slug: TUESDAY · 10:12 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — HIS ROOM
body: Theo left at eight with the teacup held out in front of him in both hands, at the height of a ring on a pillow, Hollis inside it. “I’m at the house tonight,” he said from the doorway. “Sigma Rho. I’ll be back at two. Hollis is coming with me.” What he left is the cup’s ring on the nightstand, a pale circle in the dust where the egg has spent his retirement.

The front desk at ten past ten is one fluorescent tube and Priya, on duty under a corkboard of flyers for things that have already happened, with the guest log on a clipboard and a pen behind her ear. Skye comes in through the glass doors from the curb with her keys still in her fist and her hair coming down out of its Mass pins, in the gray cardigan, buttoned to the throat. She signs where Jack points. She does *Purpose* fast, with a loop on the end, like she’s signing a headshot.

body.title: Delgado Hall — Guest Log
body.text: Resident: J. Costigan · Room: 412 · Guest: S. Callender · In: 10:12 PM · Purpose: Candlemas

body: Priya reads *Purpose*. Her eyes come up to Skye, and go across to Jack, and whatever she was going to say about the feast of the Presentation she puts back in the drawer. “I’m going to need you to sign out by two.”

He takes Skye’s hand and takes her up the east stairs. He asked her. On the church steps, with the wax gone white on her thumb and the candles still going in the courtyard behind them, he asked her up, and she looked at him and said yes like she was writing it down.

On the landing between three and four, where the light buzzes in its cage and the fire door’s wire window shows an empty hall, he stops and turns her against the rail and tells her what he wants before she can open her mouth. He can do that now — a whole sentence, his eyes on hers, nothing mumbled at the floor: he wants her against his door, and his mouth on her, and he wants her not to make one sound. Skye opens her mouth, and shuts it again, and goes up the last flight ahead of him so fast he has to let go of her hand.

412 is dark except for the parking lot. The sodium lamp out there comes in through the four inches of window he left propped and lays an orange panel across the floor and up the wall, and that is all the light there is. He locks the door behind them, and the bolt is loud. Under the window the radiator clanks as the heat comes on, a sound like somebody dropping a wrench two floors down, and goes quiet.

She has never been here. Every time it has been hers — her car, her room, her bath, her beach — and now she stands in the middle of his floor in her church clothes and takes it in: the narrow bed with the crucifix over it, the porch on Glenwood in a drugstore print with Ma’s thumb in the corner, Theo’s princes, the ring on the nightstand where an egg used to live.

body.text: On his desk, standing in a coffee mug, unlit, is her Candlemas candle, where he put it when they traded.
body.else: On his desk, standing in a coffee mug, unlit, is his Candlemas candle, for Nonna.

body: Rosie’s drawing has slipped on its tack again. Skye puts one finger to the corner and sets it straight. “Who’s the tall one?”
“Me. Rosie did it at Christmas.”
She leaves it straight and turns around, and he has her by the hips.

He turns her and puts her back to the door, and the door is the only thing separating them from the fourth floor: a slab of painted particleboard, and on the other side of it the hall carpet, Doug’s door, the fire door at the end that bangs every time anybody takes the stairs. Through the wall Doug’s keyboard goes in long patient bursts. Every sound in this building goes everywhere. Jack grew up in a house like that, one bathroom and a heating duct that carried everything.
He says her name, not loud, and her hand comes down over his mouth before the name is finished. She shakes her head at him, slow. Cinderblock.

So he undresses her without a word. The cardigan first, every button from the throat down, and the white collar under it, and he puts his mouth to each thing he uncovers — the notch of her throat, the top of her breast, the soft place under her arm that makes her jerk against the wood. When her hands come for his shirt he takes them and puts them back on the door beside her hips, and she leaves them there. He kneels on his own floor and takes the rest of her clothes down with him.

She has the heel of her hand jammed against her mouth before he’s even touched her. He puts his mouth on her and she shudders the length of the door. He knows the way by now and goes the long way anyway, slow, unhurried, until her other hand is in his hair and her thighs are shaking against his shoulders and the heel of her hand isn’t enough — a sound starts somewhere in her chest — and he reaches up without stopping and covers her mouth with his own hand, and she bites the side of it.

Out in the hall somebody comes up the stairs. The fire door bangs. Flip-flops, slapping, coming this way, and a girl on a phone: *no, he said that, to her face* — and they freeze, Skye flat to the door with his hand over her mouth and her heartbeat going into the wood, and the flip-flops come past 412 close enough to touch, and keep going, and down the hall a door opens and shuts.

He doesn’t stop for the flip-flops. Maybe that’s what does it. She comes with her teeth in his hand and her knees going, the door taking her weight, shaking from her shoulders down with the work of keeping it in, and the only noise in 412 is the latch, rattling very softly in its plate.

Afterward she stays up against the door because the door is the only thing doing any work. He’s still on his knees. She looks down at him in the orange light, breathing through her nose in long ragged pulls, her hair across half her face, and she takes his bitten hand off her mouth and turns it over and looks at the marks, a neat half-moon of them along the edge of his palm, already purpling. She kisses them, one at a time, like she’s counting them for the record. Then she puts the hand back over her own mouth, and holds it there, and nods at him: *again*.

He gets her to the bed. It’s extra-long and narrow as a cot, made this morning by a man who wasn’t expecting this, and he lays her down on it under the crucifix. He knows it’s there. He doesn’t look up at it and he doesn’t pretend it isn’t.

And he makes her wait. Skye Callender doesn’t get made to wait — not by a maître d’, not by a network — and she finds it out by degrees: his hands everywhere but where she wants them, the inside of her elbow, the backs of her knees, the long ladder of her ribs, his mouth following and going slower each time she arches for it. Her eyes say a great deal. She can’t say any of it. Through the wall Doug’s keyboard goes, and stops, and goes. Her hips come up off the mattress and he puts them back down.

She tries to take it back once. Her hand goes for his belt, quick and sure, the way it has every time before, and he catches her wrist on the way and lays the hand down flat on the sheet beside her hip and leaves his own on top of it until she stops pulling. She glares up at him. In the light from the lot she mouths something at him, slowly, so he can read every syllable of it, and it is not a word they say at Mass. He shakes his head at her, and goes back to the inside of her knee.
She gets a fist in the collar of his T-shirt, hauls him up to her, and whispers it against his mouth — *now* — and waits.

He keeps her waiting a little longer. When he gives it to her it’s with his hand between her legs, slow and sure, taking his time, and she comes again with her face turned hard into his shoulder and her teeth in the cotton of his T-shirt.

When she can move she rolls him onto his back and gets his belt open one-handed and takes him in her mouth. He gets his forearm across his own mouth and bites down on it. She is slow about it, slower than he was, like a debt she means to pay with interest, and he lies under the crucifix with his arm across his face and his free hand spread on the cold cinderblock over the bed —
— and the bed frame hits the wall. One flat wooden knock, straight through the block into Doug’s room.
Doug’s keyboard stops.

They freeze. Skye with her mouth off him and her eyes enormous in the orange light, Jack with his arm across his face. Five seconds. Ten. The keyboard starts again. Skye puts her forehead down on his hip and laughs without any sound at all, shaking with it, and that sets him off, and for a while they lie there in a heap, shaking with the work of not making a sound.

After that he puts her on her back, because the bed has room for one way of doing this and he has decided which. Nothing on either of them now. He comes down over her on his forearms, his weight held off her, his knees between hers, and the cinderblock is cold against his knuckles where one hand has found the wall above her head. She draws her knees up along his ribs. They kiss with their mouths open and no sound in it, and every slow slide of him along her takes him back to the edge she left him at and keeps him there, and her with him; he can feel what it does to her in the lift of her hips and the breath she won’t let out. Nobody’s hands are holding anything. Hers are spread flat on his back; his are braced, one in the pillow by her face and one on the wall. He has never been this close, and there is nothing keeping the last inch but that he hasn’t moved it, and he can feel how little it would take. It would hardly be a motion.
His mouth is at her ear. On his own bed, under his own crucifix, with the candle on the desk and his brother twenty-three since this morning, he does not know if he would say no tonight.

choices.text: “I don’t know that I’d say no tonight.”
choices.key: In your room, on your bed, you told her you didn’t know that you’d say no tonight. She didn’t ask.
response: He says it into her ear, a whisper, every word of it, and doesn’t take any of it back.
She goes still under him. Her breath stops; her hands on his back stop; her heel on the back of his calf stops. All he can feel moving in her is her heart, hard, through his own chest.

choices.key: In your room, on your bed, you told her to ask you. She didn’t.
response: Breathed against her ear, and he means it.

She goes still under him. She pulls her head back on the pillow far enough to see his face in the light from the lot, and looks at it, and keeps looking, and her hand comes up and rests along his jaw.

choices.text: *Tell her about the swing — what she told Danny — and hold her.*
choices.key: In your room, on your bed, at the edge, you told her what it was to hear her tell Danny about Montecito, and held her. She didn’t ask.
response: So he tells her that, with his mouth in her hair: that he was about to leave the den too, that night; that he crossed it before he could talk himself out the door; that he didn’t know she kept the book. Then he has nothing left to whisper, and he gets his arms around her and holds her against him, hard.
She pulls back far enough to see him. Whatever is in his face, she looks at it, and hers doesn’t hide what it does to her.

choices.text: *Say the no before she has to choose.*
choices.key: In your room, on your bed, at the edge, you said no before she had to choose. She wasn’t going to ask.
response: “Not tonight,” he whispers, before anything else can get said, before she has to choose a thing.
“Show-off,” Skye whispers against his throat, and her hands on his back don’t let go.

s09a.slug: TUESDAY · 11:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — TO THE LETTER

body.text: “No,” she whispers. “You don’t get to hand it to me like that.”
“I know,” she whispers. “I could tell. That’s why I’m not going to.”
“I know what you’re not saying,” she whispers. “I’m not going to make you say it.”
“I wasn’t going to ask,” she whispers. “You beat me to it. Don’t get used to that.”

body: He rolls onto his side to give her room to breathe, and she comes up on an elbow so her mouth is at his ear, and gives him her reasons fast and low, counting them off on his chest with one finger.

“One. Not in this bed. Not the first time. It’s an ironing board with a crucifix over it, and I have *some* manners.” Her breath is hot and quick against his ear. “Two. It’s your brother’s birthday. I talked to him this afternoon. I told him to call us. I’m not doing it on Danny’s birthday.”
The finger stops on his breastbone.

“Three.” The speed goes out of it. “Tomorrow night you walk into that little room at eight o’clock and tell him you won’t, and I want you to be able to mean it when you say it. I’m not going to be the thing that makes you a liar in there.”
She puts her forehead against his temple.
“When I ask again,” she whispers, “I want you to have nowhere to be in the morning.”

body.text: The only no in the room is his, said early, to a question nobody put. Nothing has been asked.
He offered, and she wouldn’t take it out of his hand. Nothing has been asked.
Nothing has been refused. Nothing has been asked.

body: He lies there with his hands open on her back and all of it in them, and he takes a breath to say something, and holds it. Her hand on his back goes still at it. She puts her mouth over his, and whatever it was for stays where it is.
So the line stays where it was, and everything else goes on up against it, at the same heat, without a sound.

Then he puts her on her back again. He keeps the pace, and she gives it to him. He takes her wrists and lays them on the pillow above her head — not holding them, only putting them there, the way he put her hands on the door when they came in — and she leaves them, and watches him with her mouth open in the orange light. He moves against her, the length of him along her and never into her, slow, so slow it is a kind of argument, and every time her hips come up to hurry him he waits until they settle and starts again. Her ankles lock at the small of his back. The bed wants to tell Doug about it; he finds the rhythm it won’t announce, slower than anything he would have chosen, and keeps it. She bites her own lip white. He puts his mouth over hers to give her somewhere else to put it.

Nothing in the room gets to make a sound, so everything goes somewhere else. Her breath goes out through her nose in short hard bursts against his cheek. His goes into the pillow. The cords stand out in her neck; her hands open and close on the pillowcase above her head and stay there, because he put them there. Sweat comes up along her hairline and in the hollow of her throat, and he puts his mouth to it and tastes salt and the last of the church on her, wax and the cold water off the aspergillum, gone warm. The lamp in the lot lays a bar of orange across his knuckles on the cinderblock. Through the wall Doug has stopped for the night, and the quiet on the other side of the block is worse than the keyboard was: it might be listening. They keep it anyway, the two of them, the hardest either of them has ever had to hold anything still, and it is the noise they are holding.

It takes a long time, longer than anything has. Twice she gets close and twice he feels it coming and slows, and the second time she turns her face into her own arm and shakes her head at him, furious, and takes her hands back off the pillow and puts them flat on the small of his back and holds him to it herself. After that it’s neither of their pace. It’s the one they both have.

When it comes it comes for both of them inside the same few seconds, mouths sealed, her cry going down his throat and his down hers, her heels digging in, his palm braced flat on the cinderblock over her head, the block cold and nothing else in the room cold at all; and the bed frame that told on them once tonight keeps its mouth shut. Afterward he stays over her on his elbows with his forehead on hers, both of them wet and shaking in a room with the heat on, and he can feel her heart through his own chest, slowing a beat at a time, and the cold of the wall still in his hand.

They don’t sleep. She traces the scar through his eyebrow with her thumb, and he traces the horse she drew on his ribs on Monday morning, faded now to a gray ghost of a horse, and through the wall Doug logs off with a sigh you can hear through cinderblock.
The radiator knocks at one.

It goes off under the window like a hammer on a pipe, and the two of them come up off the mattress the way you come up when a cruiser’s lights go on behind you — Skye halfway to sitting with the sheet clutched to her chest, Jack’s heart going like Ma just opened the door. Their eyes go to the radiator. Neither of them laughs this time. They stay where they are, the two of them propped up in the dark with their hearts going, until the pipe has ticked itself out, and then she lies back down on his chest, very carefully, as if it might go again. “I am never sleeping here,” she whispers. “I’d die.” She doesn’t move.

s09b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE QUESTION UNDER THE CRUCIFIX
body: After that, the streetlight. The lot lamp has the room to itself: up the wall and across the bed and over the two of them, and the crucifix above them turned dark copper. His arm is under her neck and has been asleep since before the radiator, and he doesn’t move it.
Skye lies on his chest with her chin on her hands and looks up at the crucifix — the small bronze body, the wood behind it, the lamp on both. She looks at it a while and doesn’t make a joke.

Then she does Danny’s laugh into his chest. Badly. A wheeze with a motor in it, the air going out of him in pieces, and Jack has to pull the pillow over both their heads, and from under it, muffled: “Sorry, sir. Family news.”
When the pillow comes off she’s smiling. She puts her chin back on her hands.

body.text:
“He called me Mary Catherine,” she says.

“Gina.”

“Gina,” she agrees. “Gina’s a wire service.” She thinks about it. “My mother doesn’t even call me that. She says *Skye* on the phone when it’s only us, in case somebody’s listening. Your brother’s on a recorded line in a prison, and he said it anyway.”
body.else: “He said yeah,” she says. “When I said call us. On a recorded line, in a prison. I think that’s binding.”

body: “Extended forecast,” she says to the crucifix. “Thursday: Hale, partly cloudy. Sunday: football, with a chance of you yelling at Tomás’s radio again.” She stops there, and puts her hand over his heart.
“Is there a version of later I’m in,” she says. “If I never believe it.”
He starts to answer and she puts a finger on his lip.
“Not the logic. I have the logic. I know what it says about mixed marriages; I read the section on my phone in the makeup chair.” Her finger doesn’t move. “The *thing*.”
She turns her head and lays her cheek on his chest, facing the window.

“My father married my mother in a church,” she says. “St. Mary’s, in Lancaster. Pat Doyle. He had a rented suit for it — there’s one picture she didn’t cut him out of. He was gone by the time I was four.” The lamp buzzes outside, faint. “So I don’t think the church part is what keeps anybody. I know that’s not an argument. I know you could take it apart in your sleep. It’s just the only wedding I’ve got.”
He doesn’t take it apart. He puts his hand in her hair and leaves it there.
Down in the lot a car door shuts, and somebody’s keys, and then nothing anywhere on four.
She lifts her head to say the rest. “I watched you kneel tonight,” she says. “Everybody went up and you stayed down, and I held your candle. I liked holding it.”
Her hand stays flat on his chest, over the horse that’s nearly gone.
“But I can’t go up with you. Not if I don’t believe it. That’s the one thing I won’t fake, Jack. Not for anybody. Not for you, especially.”
Her ear goes back down over his heart, and stays there.

choices.key: Under the crucifix Skye asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. You told her what Nonna said: Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife.
response: “Sunday night,” he says. “After you fell asleep on me. Gina texted, one in the morning, Nonna had woken her up to send it.” He tells her the rest: Nonna says *Maria Caterina* is a good name for a wife.
Skye goes very still on his chest. He feels it go through her and stop. “Your grandmother’s never met me.”
“She’s lit two candles.”

She’s quiet so long he hears the elevator go down to the lobby and come back up empty. When she speaks it’s with a little lift in it, a girl being fine: “Tell her it’s a good name for a lot of things.” And then, with her face turned down into his neck where he can’t see it, with no lift in it at all: “Tell her thank you.”

choices.key: Under the crucifix Skye asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. You told her she’s in all of it.
response: “All of it,” she says. She turns it over. “That’s a big part.”
“You’re a big actress.”
She smiles; he can feel it on his chest. When it goes she lifts her head. “Don’t give me all of it if you don’t have it, Jack.”

“I have it.” And because she’ll want the specifics, he gives her some: Sunday Mass with her beside him. Glenwood next Christmas, Nonna feeding her till she can’t stand up and then feeding her standing. Danny calling and asking for her first. “All of it,” he says. “I wasn’t rounding.”
She looks at him. She puts her head back down over his heart and lets him have said it.

choices.text: “I don’t know how it works yet. I want it to.”
choices.key: Under the crucifix Skye asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. You told her you don’t know how it works yet, and you want it to.
response: “I know what the Church says about it,” he says. “I could cite you the canon. I don’t know what it looks like in a kitchen on a Tuesday. I want to find out.”
“That is a very Catholic sentence,” she says. “*Wanting it to.*”
Her fingernail starts on his ribs, over what’s left of Monday’s horse, going around and around the same line.
“Find out,” she says into his chest. “I’ll wait. I’m bad at waiting.” The fingernail stops. “I’ll do it anyway.”

s09c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:45 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH FLOOR → THE LOBBY
body: They dress in the orange light with their backs half turned. It’s ridiculous after everything, and she says so, and does it anyway. The white collar. The gray cardigan, buttoned wrong, and undone, and buttoned right. Her hair twisted up off her neck and stuck through with a pen from his desk.

body.text: On her way to the door she passes the desk and her candle standing in its mug in the streetlight, and touches the wick with one finger as she goes by.
body.else: On her way to the door she passes the desk and his candle standing in its mug in the streetlight, Nonna’s, and touches the wick with one finger as she goes by.

body: He walks her down. The fourth-floor hall at a quarter to two is brown carpet and shut doors and the exit sign humming red at the far end, and halfway along it, where the hall opens out, the lounge is lit.

Theo is in it. So is Laney, cross-legged on the couch in a Pi Lam sweatshirt with a yellow highlighter crosswise in her teeth. So is Margot at the long table, a notebook open in front of her and the pen held over it, uncapped. So is Kevin, in plaid pajama pants and a hooded sweatshirt, with his arms folded so tight it looks structural. And the whiteboard on its rolling stand: as Jack and Skye come level with the doorway, Theo puts a hand to it and sends it spinning on its pivot so hard it keeps going — blank side, writing side, blank side. On the way around Jack gets a column of names in three colors of marker, and under it a car: four wheels, and inside it six circles.
Everybody in the lounge holds still. The whiteboard doesn’t.
“Book club,” Theo says. “*Dubliners*.”
Margot, without looking up from the notebook: “Science.”
“Hi, guys!” says Kevin, sunny and in pain. “I’m here under protest.”
Laney takes the highlighter out of her teeth long enough to say “Evenin’,” to Skye, in a voice like a frost advisory for the Panhandle, and puts it back.
The whiteboard comes to rest blank side out and rocks a little on its casters.
At the stairwell door Skye looks back over her shoulder at the lit doorway, mild as milk. “Somebody’s running lines,” she says. “Big cast.” And she takes the stairs.

In the lobby Priya is asleep over the guest log with her cheek on her forearm and the pen still in her fingers. Skye slides the clipboard out from under her elbow without waking her and signs herself out — *Out: 1:52* — and then, next to *Purpose*, writes something more, small and quick, and slides the clipboard back under Priya’s arm, and Jack gets as far as *Pur—* before it’s gone.

The Saab is at the curb with the top up and the windows fogged from the inside. He gets in the passenger side to say goodnight with the doors shut, and she kisses him across the gearshift with the engine running and her hand fisted in the front of his T-shirt, long and slow, the gearshift digging into his ribs. When he gets out she leans across the passenger seat to the open window and looks up at him.

body.text: “Two candles,” she says, and goes.
“All of it,” she says, and goes.
“Find out,” she says, and goes.

body: He takes the east stairs back up. On four the lounge is still lit, and as he comes past, the door is swinging shut on its arm, and through the last of the gap comes Laney’s voice, low and fast and urgent — “— she’d *decided*, Theo —” — and the door closes on it.

In 412 he gets into bed in his T-shirt. The pillow smells like her shampoo and the room smells like the radiator. The crucifix is a dark shape on the wall over him, and the lamp in the lot hums, and his hand, where she bit it, is sore.

Theo comes in at 2:20 without turning on the light. He says nothing. Jack hears his shoes come off, one and then the other, and the springs of the other bed, and last, very carefully, the teacup set back down on the nightstand in its own ring.

s10.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY — THE LEGAL PAD
body: Morning comes into the Delgado lobby through the glass front doors and lies in one long bright slab across the linoleum to the mailboxes, where it finds every fingerprint on the little brass doors. The night guest log is gone from the front desk. In its place a sophomore in a lanyard is doing the *Tide* crossword in pen, and somebody’s bike leans against the bulletin board directly under Priya’s laminated sign forbidding exactly that.

Jack’s box has one thing in it: a half-sheet of goldenrod from the Newman office, ST. BLAISE · THROATS · TODAY AT 12:10, over a clip-art pair of candles crossed into an X. Yesterday’s candles. Mrs. Fitch wastes nothing.

Down at the other end of the wall, by the 200s, Lena Broussard is holding court with a yellow legal pad propped on her forearm like an order book. Laney is at one elbow in the quilted vest. Kevin is at the other, holding a fat fan of gas receipts in a binder clip, Chevron after Chevron from the Walk for Life van, kept for the math, with the expression of a team captain who has been made treasurer against his will.

“Beds are Dupre Street, and that is not a discussion,” Lena is saying, writing it down as she says it and underlining whatever she means to hold people to. “Mama has the attic made up, and the front room for whoever loses the coin toss, and if one of y’all says the word *hotel* in her hearing she will take it personal, and she’ll be right to. Kevin’s mama’s Odyssey. Gas split six ways, and I will be keeping the receipts, Kevin, so don’t look at me like that.”
“This is my face, Lena,” Kevin says. “I was born with it.”
“Friday. Five a.m.” She boxes it on the pad. “Not Laney’s five.”

“My five is a very *reasonable* five.” Laney puts a hand over her heart, at a volume meant to carry to the elevators. “I am just — a *road trip*, Lena Broussard. I had no earthly idea you were fixin’ to do this. None. I am as surprised as anybody in this lobby.”

The front door opens on the morning and Theo comes through it in yesterday’s shirt with a cardboard carrier and three coffees. He came in last night at twenty past two and said nothing, and he has the eyes for it. He stops dead on the linoleum.
“New Orleans?” Theo says. “Did someone say New Orleans? I’ve just come from the Commons. Directly. By the path past the fountain. I heard nothing on the way but a sprinkler.”
He holds the carrier out to Lena. She doesn’t take one. She says it to Theo, with the pen still moving on the pad:
“Mama says bring the redhead. Daddy says bring the Ohio boy.” The pen stops. “I’m only telling you what he said.”

She caps the pen, takes the receipts back out of Kevin’s hand, and is out the front door with the pad under her arm. The coffee she didn’t take stays in the carrier, and Theo frowns at it as though it has let him down personally.
Laney looks down the length of the wall at Jack. It goes on a long second, and he holds it, and this time she is the one who quits first and finds something to study in the brass doors of the 300s.
The front door has swung to behind Lena, and what Jack feels about that is relief, the kind that comes when a car alarm two streets over finally gives up. It isn’t his trip.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Monday at the seminar she sat at the far end, and Hale kept her after with the door shut. Candlemas she carried a candle in the procession. Wednesday morning in the lobby she had a legal pad and a trip — New Orleans, Kevin’s mother’s van, her mother’s house — and she said to Theo, not to me, that her daddy says bring the Ohio boy. She was only telling him what he said. It’s not my trip.

response: He folds the goldenrod into his pocket and takes the stairs.
