response: Theo takes the third coffee out of the carrier and puts it in Jack’s hand. “I’ll tell him you were moved.”

choices.text: *To the lobby in general:* “I’m not going.”
response: No one asked. Kevin, who no longer has the receipts, says “Logged” to the hand they were in. Laney looks at the ceiling.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PITCH
s11.music: Talking Heads — “This Must Be the Place (Naive Melody)”
body: At the 12:10 two of yesterday’s candles were crossed under his chin for St. Blaise, and he spent the rest of the afternoon in the Brick with Fenner’s data sheets and the goldenrod flyer for a bookmark.

By half past three 412 has been turned into an office, in the flat white light the room gets once the sun has gone over the roof. Theo’s desk is cleared to the grain, the MacBook shut, the blazer hung on the chair back, and the little speakers on the sill are playing a song Jack knows without being able to name: a jumpy guitar, a bass line that lets itself in and sits on the furniture, a nervous tenor trying to make friends. Theo stands in the middle of the floor in his shirtsleeves, the cuffs turned back twice, and waits for the door to close behind Jack.
“Sit,” he says. “It’s a pitch. The buyer sits.”
“I live here.”
“Then you know where the bed is.”
Jack sits on his bed with the bag still on his shoulder and opens his mouth.
“No. You may speak at the end. It’s in the contract.”
“There’s a contract?”
“There is a contract the moment I stand up, Costigan. It’s why I stand up.” Theo draws a rectangle in the air, corner to corner, with one finger, and taps the place where the title would go.

“Fade in,” he says. “New Orleans. Sunday night, the seventh of February, kickoff at twenty-five past five, local, the hour the light on the river goes gold. A city that has waited forty-three years for its football team to be good has just been told it can stop waiting. The Colts are favored by six, and the city does not believe in six. Every bar in the Quarter will have a priest in it, and he will be winning.” He taps the air. “The franchise was awarded on All Saints’ Day, Costigan. I looked it up. Your feast, your people, your game.”

“Logline. A football kid from a football town, who has spent every autumn of his life in a Youngstown garage being told that next year is next year, is offered the one night in history when somebody else’s next year arrives. And elects to watch it in the Fishbowl.” Another tap. “With Doug. Doug will bring a diagram. The diagram will be wrong.”
“Doug’s diagrams have a Sasquatch in them.”
“Then the Sasquatch is in the Fishbowl, and you are in the Quarter.”

“Your father has been waiting on Cleveland all his life,” he goes on, more quietly, and then catches himself and puts the volume back on. “Here is a city whose wait is over, offering to let you stand next to it while it finds out. Cast.” He ticks it off across the air, left to right. “Kevin, as Caution. Margot, as Science. Laney, as Weather.”
“And you?”
“I’m the producer. Producers are never in the picture, Costigan. It’s the great tragedy of the form.”
“Who plays me?”
“You play you. It’s a documentary.” The hand comes down. “You walked out of Sully’s for a girl. Walk back in for a city.”
It is a good speech, and Jack wants it: the Quarter on a Sunday night, a city coming apart in gold. He is also already holding the no.

choices.text: “The game’s in Miami. You’re pitching me a bar.”
response: Theo brightens. “A bar the size of a city, with a river in it.” Miami has a stadium, he allows; New Orleans has the *game*, and those are different products, Costigan, because one of them is a building. He nods the geography through and goes on exactly as before. Jack has the point and can’t find where to spend it.

choices.text: “I’m a Browns fan. ‘Once in a lifetime’ is what they say to us so we’ll renew.”
response: Theo laughs, a bark that is not in the pitch, and has to wipe the board off the air with his forearm to find his place. “Cleveland has been renewing since 1964,” he says. “I see what you did there. I want that replayed in slow motion, from the other side.”
“He admits it,” Theo says. “Let the minutes show it.”
“Still no,” Jack says.
Theo writes STILL NO on the air in block capitals, underlines it twice, and moves on to the next board, visibly pleased and not about to waste it.

s11a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:41 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PITCH
body: Theo wipes the first board off the air with his forearm and starts a second, lower and to the left, and the speech changes gear from trailer to timetable.

“Item,” he says. “Transportation —”

“Lena said all that at nine,” Jack says. “In the lobby.”

“Then you’ve seen the trailer. This is the feature.” Theo doesn’t miss a beat. “Kevin has assigned the Odyssey’s seven seats in a seating chart. It has a legend, Costigan. It has a *key*.”
“Kevin made a legend.”
“Kevin made two. One is for the glovebox.”
“Item. Sixty-one dollars a head, door to door. Item. The attic has a ghost, who is, I’m told, a Saints fan. Item. Gloria loves a pilgrimage. Her words, Tuesday, by the pie case.”
“You asked Gloria.”

“I consulted Gloria. She said *hon* in several keys, and I’ve chosen to hear a yes in at least two of them. Item. Music. Kevin has submitted a playlist. It is called *Road Trip Mix* and contains nothing recorded after 1987 and two by the Carpenters, and I have decided to admire it. Item. Kevin will drive at sixty-five. Not sixty-six. He says sixty-six is a lifestyle. Item. Margot has asked that we call the trip a field season. Item. Laney has packed for us, individually, in labeled bags. Mine says *Mr. Theodore, Medium Sparkle*. I haven’t opened it. I’m afraid of what it knows.”
“What does mine say?”
“*Costigan, Large.* Nothing else. She is extremely angry with you and extremely thorough.”

“Item. Hale.” Theo lifts his chin. “He will excuse you for an essay. I have it on authority. ‘Mr. Costigan may go, provided he writes me four thousand words on the theology of the second line, and not one of them *liminal*.’” The second line, he explains, is everyone who dances behind the band on the way home from the cemetery. “I understand it is very nearly your entire position.”
It is, annoyingly, an essay Jack would like to write. He has the first sentence before he can stop himself: the band goes out slow and comes back loose.

response: Theo gets specific. It was Monday, in the corridor outside 302, at ten past three, Hale in the green tie with the soup on it and the dog asleep on his left foot.
“Berkeley’s blanket was empty Monday,” Jack says. “I was in the room. You made that up.”
“I *anticipated* it,” Theo says.

choices.text: “Sixty-one dollars. You did math. You’ve never done math.”
response: “I had it done,” Theo says. “By Margot. For science.”
“Does she bill by the hour?”
“By the footnote. I have been told there are eleven.”

choices.text: “Kevin’s mother would let me drive the Odyssey?”
response: “Kevin’s mother asked for you by name,” Theo says, flat, and goes straight on to the next item before Jack can say anything to it.

s11b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PITCH
body: The song ends, and the next one doesn’t start; the speakers hold the room with a little hiss in it. Down in the lot somebody is trying to start a Corolla, and failing with a great deal of heart. Theo has wiped the second board off the air and draws no third. He stands in the middle of the floor with his hands at his sides. Jack has not seen them do that before.
“I need you there,” Theo says.

In five months Theo has lent him a Burberry in a storm and walked into Hale’s house with a bottle that had a story, and a dozen things between. He has never asked for anything back. He has only said it, and given no reason, and stayed where he is. Jack goes for the joke where he keeps it, and it isn’t there.

response: Theo gives him a reason. It runs to a full minute and has everything in it: Laney, who has the gas card and the schedule; Margot, who has printed the maps in three colors and will be unbearable if they go unused; a hotel in Beaumont, Texas, with a waffle iron in the lobby that Theo has seen a photograph of and believes in. Jack lets him finish. At the end of it Theo says, low and level, “Because I asked.”
“Don’t get used to it,” Theo says. He turns to the speakers and brings the music back up a notch past where it was, and stays with his back to the room until the track has gotten somewhere.

choices.text: “You’ve been on her side all month, Theo. Don’t pitch me her trip.”
response: It lands; Jack can watch it land. Monday’s office comes back to him, and what Hale said across the desk, and he has gone and done it anyway. Theo takes it with a nod at the rug, and for a moment there is nothing on the board at all.

response.text: “You told me it’s love,” Theo says. “I believed you. This isn’t about that.”

s11c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:58 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE NO

body.text: Theo looks at his empty air-board. “You won,” he says. “The points, anyway. I want that noted somewhere official.”
Theo looks at his empty air-board. “You agreed with everything I said,” he says. “That’s worse.”
Theo looks at his empty air-board. “You were funny,” he says. “Funny isn’t the same as right. You taught me that.”
Theo looks at his empty air-board. “A draw,” he says. “I hate a draw. Nobody ever made a picture about a draw.”

body: “And you’re going to say no anyway.”
“No,” Jack says. It comes out as level and easy as the time of day.
“I have a slide for this.”
“There aren’t any slides.”
“There is a slide, Costigan. It’s on the other board.” Theo regards the air where it would be. “It says *Reconsider*. In a font.” He folds his arms. “Give me the reason. I’m owed a reason.”
Twenty-eight minutes of Theo’s afternoon have gone into this: a cleared desk, a speech with a priest in it, a legend on a seating chart. Whatever Jack says next had better be the right size.

choices.text: “Thirty hours in a van with Lena Broussard. Ten days in her mother’s house. I’m not doing that to Skye, and I’m not doing it to me.”
choices.key: Theo pitched New Orleans — the Saints, the money, and for the first time in his life a favor. You said no: thirty hours in a van with Lena, and you’re not doing that to Skye.
response: Theo takes it standing up, with his chin level. He draws one last board in the air, a small one, writes nothing on it, and folds it in half and in half again and puts it in his shirt pocket. “I’ll put you down as a maybe,” he says.
He takes the blazer off the chair, and at the door he stops with a hand on the frame. “Ask her.”
“Ask who?”
“Whoever you ask,” Theo says. His shoes go off down the hall toward the elevator.
Jack sits on his bed with the bag still on his shoulder, in a room rearranged for the sole purpose of asking him something, and takes the bag off.

choices.key: Theo pitched New Orleans — the Saints, the money, and for the first time in his life a favor. You said no, because you don’t want to.
response: Theo looks at him. “That’s the first lie you’ve told me since August,” he says.

Jack has no reply, and Theo seems to have expected none. He pinches the last board out of the air and puts it in his pocket, and by the time he says “I’ll put you down as a no I didn’t hear” he is in the hall with the blazer over his arm.
“Ask her,” comes back through the doorway.
“Ask who?”
“Whoever you ask,” says the hall.
Through the wall Doug says *dude* to a screen, and the song runs out into the next one.

choices.text: “Because Kevin drives like the Rapture’s at the next exit and he wants to be found doing the speed limit. And her.”
choices.key: Theo pitched New Orleans — the Saints, the money, and for the first time in his life a favor. You made a joke about Kevin’s driving, and then said the real reason: her.
response: Theo has the blazer off the chair and is working his arms into it when Jack reaches the second half, and one arm stays in its sleeve. “The second part was the pitch,” he says. “I’ll put you down as pending.”
He gets the other arm in. At the mirror on the back of the door he squares the Sigma Rho pin on his lapel. “Ask her.”
“Ask who?”
“Whoever you ask.”
In the mirror Jack watches Theo’s face for whatever it is doing, and it is entirely occupied with the pin.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — BEHIND THE SCREEN
body: The clock over the choir loft says two minutes to eight. He is early, which in this closet is new, and he sits down in the last pew in the blue dark with his hands between his knees to work out what to do with the two minutes. The votive rack still has Tuesday in it: stubs in the sand, drips of wax down the iron, a paper drip guard somebody has not had the heart to throw out.
The little light over the closet door is on. The index card beneath it has been revised.

body.title: INDEX CARD · CLOSET DOOR
body.text:
KNOCK (GENTLY)
(AND PROMPTLY)

body: The second line is in Mrs. Fitch’s pen. He knocks gently. On the far side a rosary finds the arm of a chair, and he goes in and kneels on the worn place, with his forearm on the ledge and the bruise the gearshift left on his ribs reporting for duty.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been seven days since my last confession.”
“Seven days,” Osei says. “And at eight o’clock exactly. I had prepared a remark about punctuality. It will keep. I think you will give me the occasion.”
“That’s generous, Father.”
“It is a forecast. I was a doctor.”

He starts with Sunday night and goes on to Tuesday, in the short words, with the honest verbs. Neither takes long, and neither is small. The list is shorter than the one he carried in last week, and everything on it is further down the road.

body.text: Then the worst of it, because Osei taught him to put the worst of it last and say it flat. “Last night, in my own room, I told her to ask me.”

Then the last of it, because Osei taught him to put the worst of it last and say it flat. “Last night, in my own room, I got as close as I’ve ever been, and I said no before she could ask. I don’t know how much longer I’d have had it.”
Then the worst of it, because Osei taught him to put the worst of it last and say it flat. “Last night, in my own room, if she had asked me, I don’t know that I would have said no.”
“*I told her to ask,*” Osei says back to him, very evenly. “That is not a thing that happened to you, Jack. That is a thing you said. You were right to put it last.”

“*I don’t know how much longer,*” Osei says back to him, very evenly. “Then you said it while you still had it. That is the no of a man who found it before the night and not in it, and it is worth more than you think. It does not take back the stairs.”

“*I don’t know that I would have said no,*” Osei says back to him, very evenly. “It is an honest sentence, and a frightening one. A man should know his no before the night, not in it. My mother used to tell us: you do not test the depth of the river with both feet.”

body: “She wasn’t going to,” Jack says. “She said not in my bed, and not on my brother’s birthday, and not the night before this.”

body.text: “Then you were kept twice last night, and once by someone who was under no obligation to keep you,” Osei says. “I also saw who held your candle on Tuesday. All of it is true, and all of it is on the scale, and none of it makes the other pan lighter.”

body: He gives him Monday next, because it is shorter and the worst is already said. A red light on State Street, the top down, a song on the radio. He sang it at her at the top of his lungs, and a girl in the next lane had a phone. “No wrong meant, Father. It was a fun moment and I didn’t think it through. It’s venial. I know it’s venial. I was happy, Father. I know that isn’t a defense.”
The chair creaks twice, as if its occupant has leaned very suddenly away from something, and when Osei speaks his voice has been put back in order.
“It is not a defense. It is the best sentence you have brought me.” A cough. “I saw it. My niece in Kumasi has also seen it. Ghana has seen it, Jack.”
“Yes, Father.”

“I believe you. No wrong meant. If that were the whole of it I would send you home with a smile.” The beads move. “When I practised, I told my patients: do not take the strong medicine for the small ache, Jack. On the day of the large one it has nothing left to say to you. The words in that song are strong medicine, meant for one strong thing. You knew that. It is why you said *venial* before I could.”
“Yes, Father.”
“And it was not only the two of you at the stoplight. Who watched?”
“My sister’s homeroom. Our pastor’s secretary. My mother’s phone tree.”

“Thirty-eight seconds of you, in front of all of those. It is a short text from which to read a man’s faith, and they will read it. People take the measure of the thing from the ones who say they believe it. I do not say this to frighten you; it is the same for me, and I wear the collar. Say it was light, and say it was light of you, and leave it here. I do not want you at home counting.”
“Now.” The chair settles. “Last week I asked you, to what question. Have you found it?”
*Quale ti fa pregare?* It is where it was on Christmas night, over the beads, and he leaves the first word of it on the kneeler and passes the rest through the linen.
“My grandmother’s,” he says. “She asked me at Christmas. What makes me pray.”
“Mm.” The beads. “You said it like a man reading a translation.”
Jack opens his mouth, and the Italian is whole on the roof of it, and he shuts his mouth on it.
“I do not need the original,” Osei says. “I wish only to tell you I can hear that there is one. Now the part I may not skip. In your own words, please. The Baltimore Catechism I also know.”

choices.text: “I want to. I’m closer than I’ve ever been to not wanting to.”
choices.key: Behind the screen you told Osei you want to stop — and that you’re closer than you’ve ever been to not wanting to.
response: “I want to,” Jack says. “I’m closer than I’ve ever been to not wanting to.”
It is not what he walked up the hill meaning to say, and it is the first time he has heard it said. The beads stop.
“Then you have told me the truth, which is the beginning,” Osei says. “Most men start with the end.”

choices.key: Behind the screen you told Osei you’ll try.
response: “I’ll try,” Jack says.
It sits in the closet with nothing around it, and it looks small.
“Try is a good word,” Osei says. “It is a verb. Most of the good words are.”

choices.text: “I won’t put myself there this week.”
choices.key: Behind the screen you promised Osei you won’t put yourself there this week.
response: “I won’t put myself there this week,” Jack says. “I can see as far as Sunday.”
The beads move through a hand.
“A week is a good size for a promise,” Osei says. “Small enough to carry. Carry it.”

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:24 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: “For your penance,” Osei says, “the canticle of Simeon. *Now, Master, you may let your servant go in peace.* I read it last night, and you studied your shoes. Say it tonight, slowly, and stay with the part about letting go. Everyone thinks it is about dying. It is about a man who has been handed the thing he waited his whole life for, and opens his hands.”

Behind the linen the shadow of a hand comes up. Jack says the Act of Contrition to the end of it without being stopped, and the last of the absolution comes through the screen unhurried: *in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.*
“Amen.”
“Sunday,” Osei says, “you will come up the center aisle, and I will give you what is in the ciborium and the same face I give everyone. It is the only face I brought.”

“Jack.” Beads, once. “Last week I told you to go home. You went, and you were right to, and you are back in seven days with the same fever, a degree higher. A man who is told where to sleep has not yet decided where he lives. So tonight I tell you nothing. You know where the door is.”

Out in the nave the lamp burns red over the tabernacle and nothing else burns. Mrs. Fitch has gone and taken her lamp, and the card table stands bare under the choir loft. On the top step he sits down with the cold of the stone coming up through the Carhartt, and says the canticle to the courtyard, slowly. The olive trees stand where the candles were. At the part about letting go he stops, and says it again. His hands are open on his knees.

Behind him the hall door opens and Osei comes out locking it, his coat over one arm and the ring of keys in his hand. He stops on the step beside Jack’s shoulder and looks at the courtyard instead of at him, and remarks, as a man remarks on the weather, “Adrian tells me his dog had a difficult evening last week. He called it a seminar.”
Jack studies the olive trees.
After a moment Osei nods, as at an answer, and goes down to the lot, the limp first and the keys behind it. A small car starts, and Ocean Road takes it.
The RAZR is in Jack’s hand, the cracked hinge under his thumb.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything. Candlemas: Simeon held the child and let himself be let go. At the door he said, “I saw your concert.” Wednesday at eight I told him all of it, and the song. Ghana has seen it. He asked again, to what question, and I gave him Nonna’s. He said I said it like a man reading a translation. Absolved. Penance: Simeon’s canticle, slowly — the part about letting go. He didn’t tell me where to sleep. I know where the door is.

response: He shuts the phone on its hinge and puts it away. She said *and then you come back here*, with her ear over his heart, and he said yes to it. He goes down the hill.
He thumbs down to SKYE (MISFIT) and it rings once.
“I’m on the steps,” he says.
“Stay there,” she says. “I’m coming to you.”

body: The Saab comes up the hill in ten minutes, headlights swinging across the olive trees, and noses in under the bell tower where the light over the hall door can reach it. The tower goes up into the dark above it, the bell a black shape at the top. Behind the blue glass of the church one red point is burning, the lamp by the tabernacle, and nothing else.

He gets in. The top is up and the heater is going hard, and the car smells like her shampoo and hot dust off the vents and a cold coffee in the cupholder. Her iPod is propped against the windshield, its cord running down into a cassette adapter in the tape deck, and out of the speakers, turned low, comes one man and a guitar, singing like he’s been up all night and doesn’t mind.

Skye is in a gray hoodie with her hair clipped up. Both her hands are on the wheel, though the car is in park and facing a wall, and they’re all he can look at: the rings, the bones of the wrists, the knuckles going pale when she grips. She catches him looking and grips harder.

body.text: “This is the daylight column,” she says. “At night. It’s a technicality.”

body: “You just got clean,” she says. “I’m keeping my hands on the wheel where your priest can see them.”
The gearshift stands up out of its leather boot by his knee. She tips her chin at it. “And this is Sister Mary Gearshift. She’ll be chaperoning.”
“We’ve met,” Jack says. He has the bruise.
“She’s very strict.” Skye lowers her voice. “She’s been chaperoning this car since 1991, and nobody’s ever gotten past second.”

body.text: When he tells her what he promised behind the screen — not this week — she hears it out with her eyes on the bell tower. “This week,” she says. “I heard you. I’m the week.” She takes her hands off the wheel and sits on them, both, very upright, until he laughs. The hands go back on the wheel.

She asks if he ate. “There was a Clif bar.” “When?” “Four.” Without looking she reaches into the back with her right hand, keeping her left on the wheel on principle, and comes up with a white paper bag gone see-through at the bottom: half a burrito from the truck by the gas station, in foil, warm from riding on the floor vent. He eats it over the bag while she watches every bite.

body: He tells her about 412 at half past three: Theo on his feet, the Quarter on a Sunday night, sixty-one dollars a head, thirty hours in a van. He doesn’t say who else is riding.

Partway through she reaches down and turns the key back, and the engine shudders and stops. “This car drinks,” she says. With the heater off the windshield starts to go white, on her side only. She’s doing most of the breathing in here.
Her hands are at the bottom of the wheel, turning it a little on the leather, back and forth, as far as it goes in park. At *thirty hours* they stopped turning.
“He did the board?” she says. “In the air?”
“Erased it with his sleeve.”
“That’s his father’s. I’ve watched his father do that since I was a kid.” She taps the wheel with her rings. “What did he close on?”
“A favor. He said he needed me there.”
“He held the ask till the last scene,” she says, and nods slowly at the bell tower. “That’s a good room. That’s a very good room. And?”
“I said no.”
The hands start turning the wheel again.
“Okay. I’ve got one.” She drums the top of the wheel. “I got a pilot.”
“Skye.”
“The network’s sister studio. They want a girl who can play nineteen and look like she’s never been on television. So, obviously.”
“You’re nineteen.”

“You sound like the casting director.” The fog has reached the middle of her side. “It shoots in Vancouver. The Olympics have every hotel in the city, so they’re putting us in Burnaby, which is where Vancouver keeps its soundstages. I fly Friday morning. Two weeks.”
Jack looks at the bell tower, and then at her.
“It’s a pilot,” she says. “Pilots die. Nine out of ten, they shoot it, they test it on strangers in a mall in Burbank, and a man in a ponytail says no.”
“You want it.”
“I want it.” She says it again, quieter, to see if it’s still true. “I want it.”
“Come to Vancouver,” she says. “Stow away. I’ll pack you in my big suitcase. You’ll fold right up. Catholic spine; it bends at the knee.”
He has Hale on Monday at one. She has a call sheet with her name on it at five-forty in the morning. She takes the suitcase back with a little nod, as if he’d said so.

“So I won’t be here,” she says. “Go. Go watch your Saints win. The Colts are favored by six; I asked Tomás, and he had to go lie down. You already gave me the last one. Bring me back something terrible.”
She takes both hands off the wheel then and puts two fingers flat on his collarbone, warm from the vents, and looks at him under the hall light.
“Who knows,” she says, “maybe it’ll be good for you guys.”
She lets go and puts her hands back on the wheel, at the bottom, where they were.
It’s the Saints, he tells himself; it’s only the Saints.

Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday she drove up to St. Brendan’s and sat with me in the Saab under the bell tower with the heater on and her hands where Osei could see them. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes.

choices.key: In the Saab under the bell tower Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for Theo. He asked.
response: “For Theo,” he says. “He asked.”

“Ted asked,” she tells the windshield. “Ted has never asked anybody for anything in his life. Go.” A doubloon, caught off a float with his own two hands, and a T-shirt so terrible she’ll have to sleep in it. He promises.

She leans across Sister Mary Gearshift with her hands still on the wheel and kisses him, a quick, decent, church-parking-lot kiss, and it is exactly as quick as she means it to be. It’s the look after that runs long. When she sits back she turns the key. The engine catches, the heater comes up, the fog starts to pull back off her side of the glass, and she leaves it in park.

choices.text: “For the Saints. And your terrible T-shirt.”
choices.key: In the Saab under the bell tower Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for the Saints and a terrible T-shirt.
response: “For the Saints,” he says. “And your terrible T-shirt.”
“The worst one. Sequins. A pun. A pelican in sunglasses.” And a doubloon, which he can’t buy; it has to be thrown at him from a float, and he has to catch it.
She doesn’t kiss him. She reaches up to the fogged glass on her side and, with one fingertip, draws a fleur-de-lis: three petals and a band across the middle, the left one a little fat.

choices.key: In the Saab under the bell tower Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes because she told you to.
response: “Because you told me to,” he says.
She looks at him a long time under the hall light. “Then I’m telling you,” she says. “Go.” A doubloon, and the worst T-shirt in the state of Louisiana.

She leans across the gearshift with her hands still on the wheel and kisses him, slow, a kiss with somewhere it has to be and no intention of getting there on time. When it’s over she doesn’t sit back. She rests her forehead against his across the gearshift, and they stay like that, while the white comes in from the corners of her side of the glass and the song plays out low through the tape deck.

s13p.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:05 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING
s13p.music: Townes Van Zandt — “If I Needed You”
body: The porch light is off, so the porch gets the living room instead: a long yellow panel through the screen door, laid across the boards and up one leg of the swing. Tomás has a record on in there, low. One man and a guitar, and a voice for the last person still awake in the house. Three doors down a party is losing at beer pong at the top of its lungs, and under all of it the surf comes in at the foot of the bluff and drags its gravel back out.

Skye is on the swing in a ski jacket that has never seen snow, zipped to the chin, her knees pulled up inside it and her hair down. When she sees him at the foot of the steps she pats the empty half of the seat.
“Here,” she says. “That was the rule. And then you come back *here*. I gave you the address.”

He sits, and the swing takes him and sways and settles. She unzips the jacket far enough to get her hands out, takes both of his, and lays all four out on her knees in the light from the door, his on the bottom and hers on top, neat as a stack of mail.

body.text: “This is the daylight column,” she says. “At night. It’s a technicality.”
body.else: “This is daylight,” she says. “I’m told it’s good for you.”

body: “You just got clean,” she says. “I’m keeping my hands where your priest can see them.” She lifts the stack into the light, for the street and the party and the kid going by on a beach cruiser with a speaker in his basket, and sets it back down.

Her knee, through the ski jacket and his jeans, is the only other part of her touching him. He knows where it is at all times. He has wanted to kiss her since the foot of the steps, and all of the wanting has gone down into his hands, and she has his hands.

body.text: He tells her what he promised behind the screen: not this week. She hears it out with her eyes on his. “This week,” she says. “I heard you. I’m the week.” She takes her hands back and sits on them, both of them, bolt upright on the swing, until he laughs. She gives them back.
body.else: She asks nothing about the confessional. She asks if he ate. “There was a Clif bar,” he says. “Around four.” “That’s a wrapper with ambitions.” From the far end of the swing she produces a paper plate with another paper plate upside down on it, and under that half a quesadilla Tomás made at seven, cold now and stiff as a shingle. He eats it in four bites with one hand, because she won’t give him back the other.

body: He tells her about the pitch: Theo on his feet with the speaker going, a whiteboard drawn in the air and wiped off with his sleeve, the Quarter on a Sunday night, thirty hours in a van. He leaves out who else is in the van.
Her thumb has been going back and forth across his knuckles since he sat down. Somewhere around the van it stopped.
“He drew it in the air,” she says. “The board.”
“And wiped it off.”
“With the sleeve. That’s his father. His father does that in every room he’s ever walked into.” She shakes her head at the yard. “What did he close on?”
“A favor. He said he needed me there.”
Skye whistles, low, through her teeth. “He saved the ask for last. You always close on the ask. Ted’s been in rooms.” She looks at him. “And?”
“I said no.”
The thumb starts again.
“Okay. My turn.” She sits up straighter. “I got a pilot.”
“Skye.”
“The network’s sister studio. They want a girl who can play nineteen and look like she’s never been on television.” She points at herself with their stacked hands. “So, obviously.”
“You’re nineteen.”

“That’s what I said. They said, *exactly*.” The swing creaks. “It shoots in Vancouver. The Olympics have every hotel in the city, so they’re putting us in Burnaby, which is where Vancouver keeps its soundstages and its Best Westerns. I fly Friday morning. Two weeks.”
Under hers his hands close on their own, and she pats them back open like a dog she’s teaching to stay.

“It’s a pilot,” she says. “It’s nothing. It’s fourteen hours a day in a trailer for four minutes on camera, and a hotel bar full of network men saying *love it* about things they don’t. Pilot season is a cattle call where the cattle have agents.”
“You want it.”
“I want it,” she says, and looks a little surprised at herself.
“Come to Vancouver,” she says. “It rains. There are mountains, allegedly; no one living has seen them. You could hold a boom mic. You’d be a terrible boom operator. You’d lean in.”
He has Hale at one on Monday. She has a call sheet. The bit runs out down the steps and off along Del Playa after the kid on the cruiser, and she watches it go.

“So I won’t be here anyway,” she says. “Go. Go watch your Saints win. The Colts are favored by six; I looked it up; I took notes. You already listened to the last one on Tomás’s radio on these steps because of me. I’m not taking the Super Bowl off you too. Bring me back something terrible.” She squeezes his hands. “Who knows, maybe it’ll be good for you guys.”
She says it easily, to his face, in the yellow light, her thumb going steady across his knuckles in time with the record.
He tells himself it’s the Saints, and only the Saints.

Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes.

choices.key: On the swing Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for Theo. He asked.
response: “For Theo,” he says. “He asked.”

“Ted asked,” she says. “Ted’s never asked anybody for anything. Go.” She wants a doubloon, a real one, off a float, caught by him personally, and a T-shirt so terrible she can’t wear it outside the house. He promises both.

She leans over the stack of hands and kisses him, small and closed, and sits back with her eyebrows up at herself, as if she’s surprised she stopped. The chains creak and settle. Inside, the needle lifts off the end of the side, and Tomás turns the record over.

response: “For the Saints,” he says. “And your terrible T-shirt.”
“The worst one,” she says. “Sequins. A pun. A crawfish in some kind of situation.” And a doubloon, which can’t be bought; it has to be thrown at him, and he has to catch it.

The kiss starts out decent enough to show a priest and runs long, her fingers tightening on his in the stack until he can feel her rings. When she sits away she reaches up and pulls his collar straight.

choices.key: On the swing Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes because she told you to.
response: “Because you told me to,” he says.
She looks at him a long time in the light from the door. “Then I’m telling you,” she says. “Go.” A doubloon, and the worst T-shirt in Louisiana.

She kisses him with their hands still stacked on her knees, and when it’s over she doesn’t sit back. She leans her forehead against his, and they stay that way on the swing, breathing, while the man on the record finishes the song.

body: The east stairwell has one bulb, a Spring Rush poster, and a landing where the cold comes up from the loading dock. Jack sits on the fourth step with the RAZR open in both hands. Theo is forty feet away behind a door, and it seems important that this go through a carrier.
Priya comes up from the third floor on her rounds with a flashlight she does not need, in a stairwell with a bulb, and stops two steps below him.
“The stairwell is for egress,” she says. “It is not a lounge.”
“I’m egressing.”
“You’re composing.” She puts the flashlight on the phone, courteously, and then on the ceiling, and goes up past him. “I’m not going to say anything. I’m going to remember it.”

body: He sends it. Nothing comes back, and he hadn’t wanted anything to.

412 is dark but for the streetlight, coming through the one window in a long orange block and lying across Theo’s bed. Theo is in it in his shirt, facing the wall, the blanket pulled to his ear, and over his empty desk Rosie’s princes have their crayon crowns lit. On the nightstand, in its ring, the teacup, and Hollis in it, keeping his vigil. Jack gets the door to without the click and has one shoe off when the wall speaks.
“Kevin drives the first shift,” Theo says. “You drive West Texas.”
“Who decided that?”
“There’s a chart.”

He doesn’t turn over. He laughs, quietly, into the pillow: a breath through the nose, and then a second one behind it. On the nightstand, beside the teacup, his iPhone lights face-up, and the glow slides across the ceiling and fades.
Jack gets the other shoe off and lies down in his clothes.

body.text: On the desk, standing in its coffee mug, unlit, is her Candlemas candle, the wax gone white down one side where it ran over her thumb.
body.else: On the desk, standing in its coffee mug, unlit, is his Candlemas candle, the one he is keeping for Nonna.

body: Across the room Theo’s breathing has gone slow and even a good deal faster than anyone falls asleep. Jack lies on his back with his shoes on the floor and looks at the candle until the wick, a small dark stroke at the top of it, is the only part he can see.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas.
